entry.title: Van Rysel RCR-R Pro Drops to a 705g Frame and 6.6kg Complete Bike
entry.content:
Van Rysel has a new lightweight race bike for 2027, and this one has already won a Monument.

The new RCR-R Pro gets a claimed 705g frame, more aero shaping, and complete builds starting at just 6.6kg. Alongside it, Van Rysel is launching the RCR-R, which uses the same frame design with a less expensive high-modulus carbon layup and a claimed 883g frame weight.

Both bikes go on sale January 5, 2027, with European pricing spanning €3,299 to €8,499 depending on build.

If the bike looks familiar, there’s a reason. Paul Seixas and the Decathlon CMA CGM team have been racing prototypes since June, including at the Tour de France. Seixas eventually rode the bike to victory at Il Lombardia before Van Rysel officially took the covers off. Not a bad final round of prototype testing.

RCR-R Pro: Aero Enough, Light Enough

Van Rysel already has a dedicated aero bike in the RCR-F Pro. The RCR-R attacks the problem from the other direction.

Rather than building the most aerodynamic bike possible and accepting a weight penalty, Van Rysel started with a lightweight race platform and added more aero performance. The goal is a bike that makes sense when the race starts flat, heads into the mountains, and finishes with a sketchy 90km/h descent.

The top-level RCR-R Pro frame weighs a claimed 705g in a size medium, with a ±5% tolerance. The fork adds another 360g. That makes it the lightest frame Van Rysel has produced.

The RCR-R Pro uses a mixture of super-high-modulus and high-modulus carbon, while the standard RCR-R sticks with high-modulus carbon and weighs 883g in the same size. Same shapes. Same geometry. Different carbon recipe. The178g frame difference will also drive much of the price separation between the two families.

13 CFD Bikes, Five Wind Tunnel Bikes, Seven Layups

Van Rysel spent two and a half years developing the new platform with Decathlon CMA CGM. The process included 13 CFD prototypes, five wind-tunnel prototypes, and seven different carbon layups before the final bike was signed off. That development focused heavily on balancing aero gains against weight and stiffness, rather than chasing one number.

The front end is designed to stay stiff under hard efforts and cornering loads, while Van Rysel intentionally allows more controlled flex through the rear. The idea is to keep the bike responsive without making it overly rigid when descending or riding rough pavement.

Paul Seixas, Nicolas Prodhomme, and Matthew Riccitello were among the riders putting prototype kilometers into the bike during team camps in Sierra Nevada (pictured above).

Seixas was particularly involved in the final development and started racing the bike during the second half of the 2026 season. Considering how that ended in Lombardia, Van Rysel probably isn’t regretting the decision.

A Little RCR-F Sneaks Into the RCR-R

Van Rysel says some of the aerodynamic thinking came directly from the RCR-F Pro.

The front end gets much more aggressive shaping than you’d expect from a traditional climbing bike, while the rear half stays relatively slim. It also has a curved seat tube that wraps closely around the rear wheel, plus a heavily shaped head tube and fork.

Van Rysel also developed a dedicated aero bottle and cage for the RCR-R. The brand claims the new setup can save up to 6.3 watts at 45km/h compared with the previous generation, using testing that included moving legs and turbulent airflow.

The bottles will be sold separately, with full details coming later.

How Light Are the Complete Bikes?

The headline build is the RCR-R Pro with SRAM Red AXS, which Van Rysel claims comes in at 6.6kg in a size medium. It’s already below the UCI’s 6.8kg minimum before adding pedals, cages, computer mounts, and the other little things that inevitably creep onto a race bike. Other RCR-R Pro builds are still impressively light.

Van Rysel RCR-R Pro Claimed Weights

  • SRAM Red AXS: 6.6kg
  • Shimano Dura-Ace Di2: 6.9kg
  • Shimano Ultegra Di2: 7.1kg
  • SRAM Force AXS: 7.1kg

The standard RCR-R gives up some weight but keeps the same frame shape.

Van Rysel RCR-R Claimed Weights

  • Shimano Ultegra Di2: 7.4kg
  • SRAM Force AXS: 7.5kg
  • Shimano 105 Di2: 7.8kg
  • SRAM Rival AXS: 7.9kg

For most riders, an extra 178g in the frameset is probably a pretty reasonable trade if the lower-tier RCR-R lands at a significantly better price. Especially when the silhouette and aero work are the same.

Two RCR-Rs, Eight Complete Builds

Van Rysel will offer four complete builds in each carbon level.

The RCR-R Pro gets:

  • Shimano Dura-Ace Di2
  • Shimano Ultegra Di2
  • SRAM Red AXS
  • SRAM Force AXS

The standard RCR-R gets:

  • Shimano Ultegra Di2
  • Shimano 105 Di2
  • SRAM Force AXS
  • SRAM Rival AXS

Van Rysel hasn’t released individual model pricing yet. For now, the company says the complete range will run from €3,299 to €8,499 in Europe. North American pricing and exact regional build availability should come closer to the January launch.

entry.title: EVOC Bikepacking Gets Storage Upgrade in New 9-15L Seat Pack BOA WP Bags
entry.content:
EVOC has been making Boa-equipped bikepacking bags since 2019. Sure, they first started very small, but EVOC soon expanded to haul more gear, too. We got a preview of the expanded, more boxy Explorer range this past spring and summer. But now that you can actually buy it, let’s dive into the details of the Seat Pack Boa WP that forms the “heart” of their bikepacking family.

EVOC Seat Pack BOA WP 9, 12 & 15L bikepacking bags

The new EVOC Seat Pack Boa WP bags are the biggest volume storage option in the brand’s bikepacking line-up. But they also tend to be the most adaptable, since you can roll them down quite far for smaller loads. And their latest adaptation of Boa wire & dial tensioning is easier than ever to really fine-tune a secure fit on your bike, helping prevent the dreaded saddlebag sway, no matter if your pack is half-empty or overstuffed.

What’s new?

The new Seat Pack features EVOC’s latest waterproof, PFAS-free material with heat-welded seams. They also get a new V-shaped mount that keys against your seatpost to provide a more secure attachment, preventing side-to-side sway. Still, the mount is quite short in height on the post, which EVOC explains makes it possible to mount the new bags even on MTB dropper posts while retaining some drop capability. And also helps on smaller bikes with bigger wheels where there’s often not a lot of clearance between the saddle and rear tire.

They also feature new reinforced side panels to provide structure and help retain the bag’s shape keep the bag in shape when you cinch down your gear. The new, more boxy-shape also makes it easier to stuff your gear deep and low in the bag, notoriously the most important step in packing a bikepacking saddlebag to minimize sway.

Tech details

  • dual BOA wire fit systems with TPU straps to easily dial-in a secure connection to saddle rails
  • V-shaped plastic seatpost mount with rubber gripper for secure, stable attachment
  • WP stands for waterproof with new PFAS-free, PVC-free 100% polyester fabric
  • waterproof roll-top closure with side buckles to adjust total volume
  • removable zigzag bungee loops on top to stow more gear
  • reflective details for visibility
  • 2-position taillight attachment lashing point
  • BOA 9L dimensions: 19×45×15cm, 530g
  • BOA 12L dimensions: 20×50×17cm, 570g
  • BOA 15L dimensions: 21×56×17cm, 600g
    (Note: EVOC website illustrations do NOT have the correct dimensions.)

EVOC Seat Pack BOA WP – Pricing, options & availability

Forming the core gear carrying capacity of the entire EVOC bikepacking range, the new Seat Pack Boa WP comes in three sizes and two colors. Pick from 9L, 12L & 15L, in classic Black or off-white Sand.

The 9L Boa bag sells for $175 / 130€, the 12L Boa for $200 / 150€, and the 15L Boa for $215 / 170€.

There’s also a simpler, smaller 7L Seat Pack Ultra that replaces the nice Boa system for bikepacking weight weenies at $150 / 95€.

Get all of them now to head out on an adventure, directly from EVOC or their dealer bike shops.

EVOCsports.com

entry.title: The Best Cycling Deals From REI’s Holiday Sale
entry.content:
REI’s Holiday Sale is back again. For your annual reminder of why it’s worth jumping on: REI has been closing all of its now 190+ physical locations across the U.S. on Thanksgiving and Black Friday since 2015, encouraging customers and employees alike to “Opt Outside.” The physical-shopping break means an earlier opportunity for finding deals online, with a sweeping sale that begins Nov. 13 (running through Nov. 23) marked by steep markdowns across numerous tried-and-true outdoor brands. 

While most markdown items benefit from 20-30% off, savvy REI shoppers will look closely at the deals for REI Co-op’s in-house brand gear. The sale also covers more than 3,000 styles sold at the store. There are plenty of big-ticket hard items like skis and snowboards, boots and bindings, tents, packs and racks. As always, REI Co-op members save more, with 20% on one full-price item and an extra 20% off one REI Outlet item (Use code HOLIDAY2026 at checkout; for exclusions and details, visit REI.com/coupon). REI Outlet shoppers can save up to 60% off select items from Nov. 17–19. 

REI Co-op members get access to additional benefits and offers, though terms and conditions apply to all:

  • Get free U.S. standard shipping (no regular customer $100 minimum required).
  • Save an additional 50% on a Hot Wax or Premium Wax at REI Co-op locations offering Snow Shop services. 
  • Earn 5% in card rewards on all purchases, even sale items, with the REI Co-op® Mastercard® .
  • Don’t have the REI Co-op® Mastercard®? Apply today and receive $30 in REI Co-op® Mastercard® Rewards approximately 7-10 business days after opening the credit card (must apply 11/10-11/23, approval required).
  • Get $150 off any REI Recommended and REI Exclusive trips over $1,500 USD. (must book 11/1–11/23 for trips 12/1-5/31/27).  

Dive in with the marked-down cycling goods that jumped out most to us. Given the wide selection of sale products, as well as depth of options (and colorways) from the inventories of proven brands, we started with ones we’ve tested and reviewed over the years. We selected some ideal gifts (at least more interesting than a standard set of new socks), plus identified a few big-ticket and high-performance products with steep discounts worth budgeting for yourself.   

PEARL iZUMi Attack Road Cycling Shoes (Women’s): $131 (25% Off)

This high-end dedicated road shoe is built on a 1:1 Composite Power Plate with a carbon insert (stiffness rating 8) that efficiently transfers power, while synthetic leather uppers stay durable and breathable. Zonal fit comes from a BOA Fit System with an L6E dial for quick midfoot microadjustments and a forefoot strap for set-and-forget tension. Dual cleat compatibility (2- or 3-bolt) adds versatility, and EVA and rubber heel bumpers with a 1 cm rise help with walking. 

Shop Now

Brooks England Flyer Saddle: $139 (25% Off)

Ideal for adventure cycling, commuting, and casual touring, this long-distance classic catches eyes with a vegetable-tanned leather top that molds to your shape over time, while treated nubuck leather shortens the break-in period. Suspension springs add cushioning on rough roads, and the steel rails and iconic Brooks backplate complete the look. At 30 ounces, it prioritizes comfort over weight savings as Brooks backs its leather saddles with a 10-year guarantee.

Shop Now

Ortlieb Gravel Pack QL2.2 Panniers (Pair): $161 (25% Off)

Built for gravel and touring loads, Ortlieb’s rugged, waterproof panniers are a good match for multiday tours and self-supported races. They hold 14.5 liters apiece, with roll-top closures and a PVC-free, polyurethane-coated ripstop nylon that stands up to weather and abuse. QL2.2 mounting hooks adjust without tools and fit racks up to 16 mm in diameter.

Shop Now

REI Co-op Trailmade Snap Fleece Mid-Layer: $52 (25% Off)

Gifting a simple, trail-ready fleece can round out your rider’s kit. The inner polyester grid adds the right warmth on cool days, and the UPF 50+ fabric wicks moisture and shields against the sun. Hidden front snaps let you vent when the climb heats up, while a zippered chest pocket, hand pockets, and a locker loop cover the basics.

Shop Women’s Shop Men’s

Five Ten Freerider Pro BOA Mountain Bike Shoes (Men’s): $127 (25% Off)

These high-grip, flat-pedal shoes pair Stealth rubber outsoles and the classic Dotty tread for strong pedal traction, with a lightweight EVA midsole for cushioning and flexibility. BOA Li2 dials allow on-the-fly microadjustments, and impact-resistant toe boxes add protection. The synthetic uppers on these all-day adventurers dry quickly and handle weather well.

Shop Now

Lazer Cerro KinetiCore Bike Helmet: $75 (25% Off)

Crossing seamlessly from paved to gravel, this versatile helmet’s KinetiCore technology enhances protection from rotational impact, and its TurnSys fit system delivers a stable, comfortable fit in seconds with a quick-snap buckle. The eyewear-friendly design lets you stash your shades without the temple arms pressing against your scalp. It has 18 vents and weighs 9.52 ounces (size medium). An optional Lazer LED light and Winter Kit (both sold separately) extend its range.

Shop Now

PEARL iZUMi Expedition Cycling Bib Shorts (Men’s): $116 (25% Off)

Storage is the standout on these well-featured bibs: two thigh cargo pockets with an interior mesh security pocket, plus rear pockets at the base of the straps. A dual-density ELITE Levitate 3D chamois helps dampen road chatter, while the soft nylon raw-edge bib upper and leg bands keep the fit seamless against skin. 

Shop Now

Vision Metron 60 RS Wheelset: $2,587 (25% Off)

Go big with your savings on this race-minded carbon aero wheelset, built entirely by hand. Hooked carbon rims run tubeless and pair with PRS hubs (V-1000), aero-bladed DP carbon spokes (21 front, 24 rear), and six sealed cartridge bearings. Vision developed it through extensive CFD analysis and wind-tunnel testing. At 49 ounces, the wheelset is compatible with Shimano HG or SRAM XDR freehubs.

Shop Now

Wahoo KICKR Smart Trainer: $680 (20% Off)

Wahoo’s V6 smart trainer maximizes your indoor riding with resistance that goes past 2,200 watts (accurate within +/- 1%), with automatic calibration, while the high-inertia flywheel, quiet belt drive, and KICKR AXIS feet recreate the side-to-side movement of riding outside. ERG Easy Ramp eases you back to your power target over 10 seconds if an interval is interrupted. Wi-Fi connectivity enables automatic firmware updates, with a Wahoo X trial included.

Shop Now

entry.title: 32″ Ventum Aura Gets Official, First MTB to Launch February 13
entry.content:
Ventum is going all in for mountain bikes, and it seems they aren’t messing around with “old tech”; they appear to be leading with very large wheels and a very aggressive silhouette.

But what does a company that has mainly produced drop-bar TT, road, and gravel bikes know about off-road racing? Maybe more than we think!

*Update at the bottom of post

Ventum 32″ Mountain Bike? 32/29 MX?

Ahead of this weekend’s Leadville Trail 100 MTB, Ventum Racing teased what appears to be a 32-inch full-suspension prototype through its social channels. The sneak peek was met with excitement, trepidation, and chuckles, but that’s a good thing, as we all know, social media rewards drama.

To be fair, we don’t know for sure that this is a 32″ bike. But the choice of an inverted fork, the prototype tires, and the general angles with a very low, negative drop stem all point towards the larger platform. Given the split image, At first it was hard to tell, but it almost looked as if this is a mega MX bike with a 32″ wheel up front and a 29″ wheel out back. That would make it easier to package the rear end and suspension travel while providing the benefits of the larger 32″ wheel up front.

But for sure, this is a full 32er prototype, right?

Why? In its 11-year history, Ventum has never produced a mountain bike. But it seems each year the brand offers more tire clearance and more off-road-friendly designs.

Plus, now that 32″ looks to be the wave of the future for Life Time Grand Prix (or at least some of them), why not give it a go? They have a seat at the very front of the 32″ race bike launches, and it will keep their athletes from racing other brands for the MTB Life Time Grand Prix races.

What Are We Looking At?

From the teaser images, the bike in question looks ready to roll, and like it has already been ridden. I wouldn’t be surprised to see a Ventum athlete on this during the Leadville 100 race.

From what is visible, the Ventum prototype looks more like a marathon or XC race bike than a trail bike. The flex-stay layout makes sense for keeping weight down, and it’s proven for lightweight XC work. The FSA wheels are for sure new, but now that we can expect more 32″ production bikes, OEM gear will follow.

The inverted fork choice also fits the current state of 32-inch development. Fork availability is still one of the harder pieces of the 32″ puzzle, but maybe not for long. The tires are a mystery, but damn if they don’t look WTB in some way to me… but I’ve been way off before.

Why Leadville?

If there is a place where a 32-inch mountain bike makes sense, Leadville is high on the list. The race is long, fast, and more marathon XC than technical World Cup track. Yes, there is a huge climb on the course that will most definitely be a drawback for anyone on a heavier bike with big wheels. But Leadville rewards momentum, staying on top of the gear, and general plowing through the course. The long gravel sections, doubletrack, and long descents will be a little check mark in the 32″ wheels corner.

Why 32″ Wheel Again?

The basic pitch is a lower angle of attack, smoother rollover, and possibly less fatigue from repeated bumps. We’ve heard it all at this point except for X amount of watts saved. However, that does not mean 32-inch wheels are automatically faster. But it does mean Leadville is a great way to get some real-world testing done, chum the water, and do it on a course that might fit the bike’s style.

For now, this is still a teaser. But man, it is a good one. Ventum may be new to mountain bikes, but choosing Leadville as the first public proving ground for a 32-inch full-suspension prototype is a great bit of marketing know-how. If the goal is to show that big wheels can carry speed, smooth rough ground, and make sense over 100 miles, Leadville is a pretty honest place to try it.

Ventum Aura Gets Official

After the initial teasing, Ventum has all but come out and introduced their new 32″ MTB called the Aura. It will roll on twin 32″ wheels with 120mm of travel, and is “purpose-built to win marquee off-road races across the world.” Ventum has given a launch date of February 13th at 24HOP (24 hours in the Old Pueblo), and they’ve set up a landing page on their website if you want to sign up for more details as they roll out.

Ventumracing.com

entry.title: Cyclist Magazine Podcast: Sean Yates on Wiggins, Lance and falling off ladders
entry.content:
Cyclist
Cyclist Magazine Podcast: Sean Yates on Wiggins, Lance and falling off ladders

This week on the Cyclist Magazine Podcast, James and Will are joined by Sean Yates, one of the hardest, most talented British riders of his generation and one of cycling’s most experienced coaches and sports directors.

Sean cut his teeth in 1981 at the infamous school of cycling hard knocks, Athletic Club Boulogne-Billancourt in Paris, before turning pro in 1982 with Peugeot, where he would ride alongside Stephen Roche and Robert Millar. Despite solid domestique performances, big results eluded Sean until 1988, where stage wins at the Tour de France and Vuelta a España put ‘The Animal’ on the British stars map.

A contract with US team 7-Eleven (later Motorola) followed, which saw Sean race alongside Lance Armstrong and Andy Hampsten. Those years were produced more fine performances, the best of which saw Sean wear the yellow jersey at the 1994 Tour de France – only the third Brit ever to do so after Tom Simpson (1962) and Chris Boardman (1994, 1997). As Sean explains, however, those years were also supremely hard for all of the wrong reasons, something which expediated his retirement as professional rider in 1996.

But like most ex-pros, Sean couldn’t stay away, and in 2001 he took up his first sports director post at Linda McCartney Racing Team, where he’d find himself briefly in charge of an up-and-coming star called Bradley Wiggins. Stints at Team CSC, Discovery Channel and Astana followed, before he took up a DS role at the newly formed Team Sky in 2010. Back with Wiggins, Sean helped steer the next great hope to Britain’s first Tour de France victory, famously ‘talking Wiggins down’ from quitting mid-Tour after a bust up with teammate Chris Froome.

Sadly the 2012 season drew to an acrimonious close, with Sean parting ways from Sky, moving to pastures new at Tinkoff-Saxo, where he’d stay until 2016.

In this episode, Sean talks candidly about his relationship with Wiggins and the split with Team Sky; the ‘All’s fair in love and war and cycling’ philosophy that helps keep professional cycling (mostly) one happy family; racing with Lance through cycling’s darkest years; falling off a ladder and having to have an eight-inch stick removed from his bowels; finally getting one over on Dave Brailsford; and how he’s still riding six hours a day, and why he’ll never stop.

We also talk about the upcoming Garmin Champions in CycleSport annual gala event, which sees cycling stars – including Sean – come together to raise money for Action Medical Research, which raises much needed funds to support cutting edge medical research in children’s diseases and disabilities.

See action.org.uk for more details including how you can support and donate.

Chat begins at 9.49

  • Listen to our chat with Sean Yates on the Cyclist magazine app or wherever you get your podcasts
  • Get the Cyclist iOS app / Get the Cyclist app on the Google Play store

entry.title: The Leather Wolvhammer is Back. Updated 45NRTH Winter Boots Land Just in Time for Winter
entry.content:
The coming winter has a bit more uncertainty than usual thanks to a strong El Nino forecast. While some may get less snow than usual, some are preparing for an epic winter. There aren’t many cycling brands out there that can conquer the cold like Minnesota’s 45NRTH. A few months ago, 45NRTH launched some new carbon fat bike rims supporting the winter fat tire cyclist. Today, they are in the news again with an update to their popular winter riding boots, the Leather Wolvhammer and the Ragnarok.

Leather Wolvhammer

That’s right, the leather Wolvhammer is back. First introduced as a limited edition collaboration with Red Wing Leather, the OG leather Wolvhammer is still one of Zach’s favorite winter cycling boots of all time due to how well the leather has broken in over the years.

To be clear, the new leather Wolvhammer has nothing to do with Red Wing, and the construction of the boot is substantially different. Now featuring a large BOA dial for the lower section of the boot and a large Velcro strap on the upper, the new boot is suggested for 0 – 25F (-18 – -4C) temperatures, though 45NRTH isn’t putting an official temperature rating on the boots due to how varied personal preference can be. Just know that the Ragnarok below sits one temperature rung above the Wolvhammer for slightly warmer conditions.

Leather Wolvhammer is available in sizes 38-48 and 50. In Canada, these will only be available through IBD, but in the U.S. they will also be available direct to consumers.

Retail: $325 ($460 CAD)

We haven’t tried these yet, so we can’t comment for sure, but the cleat pocket appears to be closer to the inboard side of the outsole, like the last gen Wolvhammer that we tested. That’s good to prevent heel rub, but potentially not so good if you’re trying to maintain the narrowest Q-factor on your fat bike. Just something to keep in mind since as soon as you put cleats on the boots to test out the position, you will likely be unable to return them.

  • New upper design with single-boot construction
  • Same 200g insulation for thermal protection
  • Premium leather upper material for good looks and protection on the outside, and a lining with a waterproof membrane on the inside for comfort and protection from the elements
  • Two-bolt pedal system for ultimate connection to your ride
  • Aero Gel foam pioneered by NASA provides non-compressible, ultra-lightweight insulation underfoot
  • BOA dial system for optimized fit

*Please note that one of the materials in the Leather Wolvhammer was exposed to PFAS, and as a result, these boots do not meet legal PFAS requirements in CA, NM, RI, and WA. While this product was not specified with DWR coating or any other restricted material, a supply chain issue resulted in small amounts being measured in the final product.

Ragnarok

The Ragnarok is still the boot for shoulder seasons with a suggested temperature range of 25F+ (-4C+). If deep winter cycling isn’t your thing, but you want something to keep your feet warm and dry up until the snow flies, these could be the ticket.

Ragnarok is available in sizes 36-48 and 50 and continues with a BOA fit system, but introduces a new lace path and a completely revised Velcro cuff.

Retail: $245 ($350 CAD)

  • Updated upper with high-quality Clarino microfiber for a supple, leather-like feel
  • New lace path for BOA to add strength to the closure and a more secure fit
  • Gray EVA midsole with black speckles
  • Neoprene ankle cuff for more flexibility
  • Same trustworthy rubber outsole with anti-slip microglass rubber blocks

45NRTH believes that winter riding can be magical. From quiet trails to crisp, cold winter air, they can equip you for all things winter. Hit the link below for all of the cold-weather gear.

45NRTH.com

entry.title: Garmin Sales Begin: Huge deals on Garmin Fenix, Edge, Forerunner Series and more!
entry.content:
Like clockwork, Garmin has put forth their sale plans for the Black Friday and Holiday season. Garmin is actually one of the most predictable companies in this space when it comes to sales and how they structure them (with Wahoo probably being *the* most predictable one). The sale prices Garmin puts forth now are essentially their deals for the holidays. They don’t tend to reduce prices on these specific products further, and don’t really add anything else. This is it, at least from a US perspective (European sales are the Wild West and field of dreams of pricing…anything is possible).

The exception to that rule in the US is Uncle Amazon. Uncle Amazon has a long history of throwing very random deals into the mix, especially over Black Friday weekend. These tend to fall into one of two buckets. The first is buckets where Garmin has basically worked with Amazon to offload huge chunks of older inventory, and you’ll see some crazy deals on that. The second is when Amazon doesn’t partner with Garmin at all, and simply decides to randomly cut the price yolo style. This is usually previous-generation stuff, but at least once or twice over each Black Friday it ends up being a newly released product.

Anyway, my advice here is simple: If you see something on sale you want, buy it now, and then if you find a better Amazon deal later, you can always return it or such. For Amazon, you can return items bought Nov 1-Dec 31st until Jan 31st 2027. As always, the random deals don’t tend to last. They’re flash in the pans. Got that?

With that, onto the deals! And thanks for supporting the site via the links below. As an Amazon Associate, I earn from qualifying purchases. Enjoy!

entry.title: The Best Gifts for Bike Mechanics: What to Get Your Favorite Repair Guru
entry.content:
Bikes are incredibly fun to ride. And for most cyclists, they are fun to work on, too. However, nothing ruins an evening wrenching in your garage more than not having a proper tool. How often have you been elbow-deep in a bottom bracket swap, with the chain, chainring, and cranks removed, only to find you don’t have the right-sized BB tool? Likely, the cyclist in your life has, which makes something on this mechanics list the perfect gift.

Keep It Clean & Easy

A clean bike is easier to work on, and the SILCA Bike Care Box Set ($100, regularly $125) gives the mechanic in your life most of what they need.

The kit includes SILCA’s Ultimate Brake and Drivetrain Cleaner, Ultimate Bike Wash, and Ultimate Graphene Spray Wax, along with microfiber towels and a foam applicator. The drivetrain cleaner handles the grimy stuff, the wash is made for painted and finished surfaces, and the graphene spray wax adds a protective finishing layer once everything is clean.

It’s a nicer take on the traditional bucket-of-bike-cleaning-stuff gift, and one that will actually get used.

A Torque On The Go

Torque wrenches are essential around carbon parts, but most aren’t something you’ll throw in a jersey pocket. The Feedback Sports Reflex Fixed Torque Ratchet Kit ($65) is small enough to travel while still handling one of the most common torque values on a modern bike.

The modular mini ratchet includes a 5Nm click-torque extension, a 25mm extension, and 10 bits covering 2- 6 mm hex, T10, T25, T30, and a 3mm flat blade.

You can configure the extension as a T-, L-, or inline handle, while the ratchet has 6-degree engagement for tight spaces. For stem bolts, seatpost clamps, cockpit adjustments, and rebuilding a bike after travel, 5Nm covers a surprising amount of ground.

Wax Without the Crock Pot

Waxed drivetrains are great. Boiling chains in the kitchen is a slightly harder sell.

For mechanics and riders who want most of the benefits without setting up a dedicated hot-wax station, some good drip options are available now.

Formula 100 Fast Wax ($24.95/120mL) uses a wax carrier designed to penetrate the rollers and pins while also adding corrosion protection. It applies like a normal drip lube, so it requires no chain removal or molten wax.

The Stan’s Polar Drip Wax & Drivetrain Cleaner Bundle ($28.50) approaches the same job as a two-step system. Clean the chain with the included Drivetrain Cleaner, then apply the water-based Polar Drip Wax. Stan’s claims more than 200 miles per application, depending on conditions.

Either is an easy, stocking-sized upgrade for the mechanic already tired of scrubbing black chain grime off everything.

Give Them Shop Air

Once you have an air compressor in the bike shop, going back to a floor pump feels unnecessarily primitive.

The California Air Tools 8010 ($240) is a particularly good garage option because it runs at just 60 dB, which is much easier to live with than the usual construction-site compressor racket. It uses an oil-free 1HP pump, an 8-gallon steel tank, delivers 2.2 CFM at 90 psi, and has wheels to move its 48-pound body around the shop.

Pair it with the Park Tool INF-2 Shop Inflator ($162.95), and you have one of those shop upgrades you’ll wonder why you waited so long to buy. The INF-2 has a dual-sided Presta/Schrader head, built-in gauge, 360-degree rotating head, and is fully rebuildable. It’s especially handy when seating stubborn tubeless tires.

Not inexpensive, but neither is spending Saturday afternoon pumping a fat bike tire to seat the bead.

Bleed Brakes Like a Pro

If your home mechanic is still piecing together brake bleed supplies from a drawer full of random syringes and adapters, the Park Tool BKM-1.2 Mineral Brake Bleed Kit ($171.95) cleans things up.

It’s designed to work with most mineral-oil systems, including Shimano, Magura, TRP, Tektro, Trickstuff, SRAM DB8, Campagnolo, Promax, and others.

The kit includes two syringes, hoses with shutoff clips, multiple bleed blocks, a funnel, syringe holders, fittings, spare O-rings, and a proper storage case. Better yet, Park makes the individual pieces replaceable, which is what you want from a tool that could see years of use.

Mineral oil isn’t included, and keep this kit far away from anything used with DOT fluid. If you’re a DOT user, you can get the same kit here for your DOT needs here.

For the MTB Suspension Mechanic

Suspension service is often the point where many home mechanics hand the bike over to a shop. The new Park Tool FSK-1 Fork Seal Kit ($259.95) helps remove one more excuse.

The FSK-1 is built specifically to remove and install fork dust wipers without damaging the lowers. It includes drivers for 30, 32, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, and 40mm stanchions, covering a huge chunk of the modern fork market.

The handle doubles as the removal tool and can be used as a slide hammer for installation. Park also includes steel and non-marring plastic removal tips, plus spares.

It’s definitely a specialty tool, but for someone servicing multiple forks each year, that’s exactly why it makes a great gift. It’s the kind of tool they want but may struggle to buy for themselves.

For The Wrench With Everything

Need something inexpensive for the mechanic who already owns everything? The Park Tool Pizzeria Cup is $5. It’s blue (not the red ones most will remember from Pizza Hut), but it still has that vibe, and we’re here for it. It holds 20 ounces, fits in the top rack of the dishwasher, and will probably become the official shop cup immediately. Just don’t pour hot coffee into it.

Got too much money to spend? At the exact opposite end of the gift spectrum is Park Tool’s TS-2.50 50th Anniversary Professional Wheel Truing Stand.

Park built just 50 of these to celebrate 50 years since the original TS-2 arrived in 1976. Each gets gold powder coating, a numbered engraved plate, custom graphics, and CNC-machined aluminum knobs featuring the original Park Tool logo.

For the Wheel Master In Your Life

Tubeless rim tape is simple... right up until you’re trying to keep it centered, maintain tension, rotate the wheel, and avoid sticking the tape to itself at the same time.

The ENVE Tubeless Tape Gun is one of those wonderfully specific shop tools made for anyone who sets up a lot of tubeless wheels. Instead of wrestling with a loose roll, the dispenser helps keep the tape controlled and tensioned as you work around the rim, making it easier to get a clean, consistent installation.

Is a dedicated tubeless tape gun necessary for the occasional home setup? Probably not. But for a mechanic, race team, or rider with enough wheels in the garage to qualify as a small shop service department, it’s exactly the sort of tool that makes a repetitive job faster and less annoying.

Pair it with a few rolls of the correct-width ENVE tubeless tape, and you’ve got a very mechanic-specific, very tubeless, holiday gift. Because nothing gives happiness quite like properly centered rim tape.

entry.title: Alpe d’Huez during the Tour de France: Cycling’s biggest party
entry.content:
Cyclist
Alpe d’Huez during the Tour de France: Cycling’s biggest party

Alpe d’Huez is by no means the Tour de France’s toughest peak. The climb is only half the length of Mont Ventoux and its summit is some 800m lower than the Col du Galibier. Neither of those climbs, however, nor any other, can match the decibels produced on the Alpe.

Over the past few decades this mountain has garnered its own legend, attracting fans from around the globe to bear witness to some of the Tour’s most defining moments. It has since become a bucket list attraction for any pro cycling fan, leading it to be branded by the level-headed newspaper L’Équipe as a ‘climb in the style of Hollywood’.

So when Tour de France organisers promised the 2026 race would have back-to-back stage finishes on Alpe d’Huez, fans instinctively scrambled for the nearest hotel rooms and campsite pitches to guarantee a double bill on the sport’s loudest mountain.

Move over Maracanã and Azteca Stadium – for one weekend this summer, Alpe d’Huez became the biggest sporting arena on the globe, with a reported crowd of half a million people there to catch a glimpse of Tadej Pogačar riding up the mythical hairpins.

Between the caravans, Europop and mankinis, Cyclist speaks to some of those who made the sporting pilgrimage.

Article continues below…

Colin

from Belgium

‘I’ve spent five nights sleeping inside a tent here. I’ve got neck pain, back pain, I’ve almost lost my voice, but it’s worth it. We’ve been having a party for the past five days, but today is the one we’ve been waiting for. People have been walking and cycling up here since 4am, so we had an early start to get the party started and make sure they didn’t miss out.

‘We have three speakers, so if one runs out of charge or breaks, we’ve always got another on standby. My favourite thing to play is the Dutch song “Links Rechts”. Everyone here knows it and it’s great to see people jumping from side to side together.

‘We were initially a group of 13, but several hundred have now come down to the corner. We’ve been chatting away and making new friends throughout the day. I remember some people from the last time I was here four years ago. That’s what the Tour’s about – making memories and connections that last a lifetime.’

Thomas, Julien, Kevin and Jordan

from Belgium

‘We’ve been in the Alps all week – around ten days already. Today we chose to dress up as Quinn Simmons because we like his character, his look, the energy, the aggression on the bike. He’s been active during every stage of the race so far.

‘We haven’t been dressed like this for ten days though. This is the first day we’ve been in fancy dress. We bought the gear off AliExpress and we have some wigs and stick-on moustaches to wear once the race gets closer. He’ll probably be dropped by the time he reaches us, but getting a high five from Quinn would be great.

‘We only got off the cable car about 30 minutes ago, but we’ve already had around 20 people ask for photos. We’re expecting a lot of extra attention – some Americans have already been quite loud.

‘We’re not sure where the best hairpin is to watch the race today, but we’ll find a way to hunt down the best atmosphere. We’ve probably had about two beers each for breakfast. We’ve got two rucksacks filled with drinks, so I reckon we have about 40 to get us through the day. We’re Belgian – the beers are never far.’

Jean-Louis

from France

‘We’ve lived in Huez since 2001 but my wife was born here. We’re not cyclists as such, but we’ve got lots of Tour memories. This year my cousin is here. We’ve never considered putting our house up on Airbnb or anything when the Tour comes. This is a moment for family and friends.

‘Every three or four years this town becomes something else. Every time, the Tour feels more popular. People flock to the bends nowadays, but I think we used to be able to get closer to the riders.

‘There are more caravans too. They’ve taken all the parking spaces in the town. Some have been parked outside our house for a week. I think there are more people this year because of Paul Seixas. I’ve noticed more French people in particular. He is our golden boy and when we have a Frenchman doing well, it sparks national euphoria.

‘We’ll have our lunch on the balcony, then head down. We might have to go earlier than that to get the best spot.’

Victor, Monica, Sofia and Claudia

from Mexico

‘We’re from Torito’s [Isaac del Toro’s] hometown. We’re almost family. She [Claudia] was his neighbour.

‘This is our fourth or fifth Tour de France. We’ve been to Strade Bianche, the Giro, Tirreno-Adriatico – there were maybe six, eight or ten Mexicans at those races. Today there are probably a couple hundred around this one corner.

‘A lot of our Mexican friends have been here for two or three days already. There’s definitely some tequila in the cool boxes around here somewhere, so if Torito wins we’ll get drunk together.

‘Isaac’s having a massive impact back home. Finishing second at the Giro created a big boom for the cycling community, but now a culture is growing around the Tour de France. Most people didn’t really know what it was about. They knew it was a race in France but nothing else. People are talking about it this time. There’s even a channel dedicated to showing maybe five or six hours of the Tour. Before, you would see just a 30-minute highlight package.

‘Even though we got knocked out of the World Cup, we are still happy because of Isaac. We’re not jealous of Tadej either. We want him to help Isaac win a Tour. Isaac will get his time.’

José, Karel and Lars

from the Netherlands

‘When the Tour route was announced, we knew we had to come here. It’s 1,200km from home but we drove it in one go. If you want a spot on Dutch Corner you have to arrive a week before.

‘A Dutch priest would ring the church bell at this corner every time a Dutch rider won on Alpe d’Huez. That’s why it’s called Dutch Corner. We came here because of that. It’s like a big orange family. It’s often the same people here year after year. We don’t know each other in Holland but when we come here we all look out for each other. That atmosphere and the music, it’s what we call gezelligheid.

‘More Dutch people were here last time we came [in 2022]. There was more atmosphere in the days before, but this year it was a bit quiet. There were maybe ten Dutch people here during the week. In 2022 there were 20 or 30.

‘Because it’s a good atmosphere people know to come here, so it often gets crowded. People get drunk and arguments start. There were some issues with the police before. It’s getting worse – and less Dutch – every year. It’s a shame.’

Ulf

from Denmark

‘We had a Danish Corner on the Col de la Loze last year. It was a big success so we felt we needed somewhere for the Danes to gather at this year’s race.

‘Some Danes started following the Tour in Barcelona. It began with just a small group of friends but word spread about Danish Corner through social media. It has moved around France. Some have been following the race since the start, but a lot of the group have been together since Stage 15 [when the race reached the Alps].

‘You can always see a Danish flag when the Tour’s on TV. I think it’s been more noticeable this year. We’ve brought a piece of Denmark to France and I think we’ve challenged Dutch Corner today. Everyone here is wearing red – football shirts, flags, it’s everywhere. One guy has even painted his moustache red. We’ve got our own Danish beers, food and Faxe Kondi – a drink we call Danish gasoline.

‘There’s great camaraderie here with hundreds of Danes looking out for each other. I have a little child at home, but when you have such good friends around, it helps with the homesickness.’

Nataša 

from Slovenia

‘I’ve been to the Giro and the basketball and football European Championships, but never the Tour de France. It’s my first time. I’ve been watching the Tour on TV since Armstrong, Pantani and Ullrich and I’d like to think that I would probably be here even if Pogačar wasn’t, but this year I have time, and I don’t want to miss my chance to see Pogi.

‘I live near his home town but I’ve never seen him race in real life before. I heard that he’s underlined this stage, so it would mean everything to see him win.

‘Every time I see Slovenian sport I wear this flag necklace. It’s from cheering at the basketball European Championship and the football Euros. I’m also wearing this hat [a sombrero] because Del Toro and Pogačar are such good friends.

‘Slovenia is such a small country, so it’s a huge opportunity for our sportsmen to put us on the map. Right now, Pogačar’s our number one. Cycling was popular before him but now even more. The clubs don’t have space for new kids. Hopefully our government will pay to host the Tour de France soon.’

Dieter ‘Didi the Devil’ 

from Germany 

‘I’ve been following the Tour in this costume for 33 years. I’m 74 now. I’ve had a couple of health issues but I’m still jumping. It’s like an addiction.

‘Fans and riders recognise me. People ask for photos and shout “El Diablo” at me. I’m not sure whether I’m a celebrity but I enjoy it. It’s my work.

‘Someone asked how much I would have if I had a euro for every photo. The truth is, I don’t make any money from that. I have sponsorships, but I’m doing it for fun really. It’s a funny life. I bring a van with me for the race. It’s got a mattress inside. I was staying in a rough area in Barcelona, however, and my van was broken into before the first stage. They smashed one of the windows and stole some of my things. They didn’t take my devil costume, but I had to miss the race.

‘I was here on the Alpe for the Étape du Tour last week. No other climb in this sport is like Alpe d’Huez. This is what cycling is all about.’

The post Alpe d’Huez during the Tour de France: Cycling’s biggest party appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: ENVE’s $125 Tubeless Tape Gun Is Basically Gift Wrap for Your Rims
entry.content:
I feel like this announcement should start like an infomercial or one of those “As Seen on TV” things. “Are you tired of tubeless tape wrecking your day? (house starts on fire) Are your hands too greasy to get proper adhesion to the rim? (drops expensive wheel, blows up) Are you also fanatical about properly wrapped gifts? Well, boy, do we have a gadget for you!” 

ENVE’s new Tubeless Tape Gun is exactly what it sounds like: a dedicated shop tool for installing tubeless rim tape quickly, straight, and with consistent tension. It looks a little like someone crossed a label maker with a caulking gun, and at $125, it costs considerably more than the roll of tape you’ll be feeding through it.

BUT before you judge – I’ve used it, and it’s pretty fantastic. It works as advertised, plus it looks cool, but that doesn’t mean we’re gonna stop joking around. Because it’s fun, and ENVE knows how to take a joke. And, annoyingly for anyone hoping this would be easy to make fun of, it works really well.

ENVE Tubeless Tape Gun

Installing tubeless tape isn’t difficult, but doing it cleanly can be a pain. On a new set of wheels, it’s more of a practice in patience. “Don’t mess up the customer’s new wheelset with a big ol’ crinkle in the tape.” It’s more of an annoying task on a well-used wheel, mostly because it means something isn’t working/sealing correctly.

When you’re re-tapping a rim, things can get messy, not only from cleaning the used rim, but from the taping process. You’re trying to keep the tape centered while maintaining tension, rotating the wheel, avoiding wrinkles, and making sure you don’t wander up the sidewall halfway around the rim.

If you’ve worked in a shop, you can do it easily, but wouldn’t it be cool to have a tool for it? The ENVE Tape Gun just makes the process cleaner and more repeatable, especially for first-timers.

How Does it Work? A shaped roller centers the tape in the rim bed while you push the tool forward and rotate the wheel toward you. A thin rear wheel pushes the tape down onto the center of the rim bed. Once you finish the lap, a built-in metal cutting blade trims the tape without reaching for scissors or a knife.

I like to think of it as one of those fancy wrapping-paper cutters you see around the holidays, except this one is made of aluminum and costs enough that your family might think you have issues.

Built Like a Shop Tool

The first thing that stood out when I used the ENVE Tape Gun was how solid it feels. This isn’t a lightweight plastic tape dispenser.

ENVE uses an aluminum skeleton, rubber grip, durable plastic guides, and a metal cutting blade (also replaceable). It feels built to survive a busy service department rather than sit at the bottom of a home toolbox.

The ENVE Tape Gun works with rolls using a 75mm / 3-inch core and accepts tape widths from 25mm to 40mm, which covers a broad range of road, gravel, and mountain bike rims.

Really….Does It Actually Work?

Yes, and damn well. The Tape Gun keeps the tape centered, maintains good tension, and makes the entire process feel much more controlled and, dare I say, easy.

For a tryout, I retaped my cyclocross wheels that badly needed a refresh. The tubeless tape was starting to dip at the edges (those not-so-flattering images above) and pull up where the tape overlapped.

The process was simple: I pulled off the old tape, cleaned the rim, and measured the old tape. It came in at 25mm, so I used the ENVE tape designed for 29mm (fitting rim inner width from 24-26mm)

What did I notice? The biggest improvement is consistency; you’re not trying to do four things at once, you’re just rotating the wheel and steering the tape.

When you’re taping wheels by hand, the first one usually looks perfect. If you’re doing more than a set, thats when things can go downhill. By wheel number six, you start negotiating with yourself about whether being 2mm off-center really matters. Then you wonder whether to trim with a razor (no) or try again.

With the ENVE Tape Gun, the process is basically the same every time.

  1. Install the tape you need for the rim width.
  2. Attach the tape to the rim.
  3. Push the tool.
  4. Rotate the wheel.
  5. “Wheelie” to cut the tape.
  6. Done.

For a professional shop, race mechanic, wheel builder, or anyone regularly setting up tubeless wheels, that repeatability is genuinely useful.

It also makes the finished job look better, and anyone who’s had to troubleshoot a slow tubeless leak knows neat tape installation isn’t purely cosmetic.

But… $125?

Here’s the problem. It’s $125. If you tape two wheels a year in your garage, there’s almost no way to make the math work. A thumb still costs considerably less.

For a home mechanic, this lands squarely in the category of “extremely nice tool that you absolutely do not need.”

For a shop, though, the argument gets easier. If you’re setting up tubeless tires every day, saving a little time and getting more consistent results adds up. The Tape Gun also feels built well enough that I’d expect it to survive years of normal shop use. Plus, if you’re an ENVE dealer, it’s a cool tool to have out and chat with customers about.

That’s probably where ENVE nailed the product. It’s cool-looking and works. It doesn’t solve a complicated problem. It just makes a repetitive job faster and cleaner. 

The Perfect Gift for the Mechanic Who Has Everything?

This might also be one of the most oddly appropriate mechanic gifts of the holiday season.

You could wrap the Tape Gun, then they can unwrap it and use it to wrap wheels.

There’s some nice symmetry there.

Jokes aside, the ENVE Tubeless Tape Gun is a genuinely excellent tool. It works exactly as advertised, feels properly shop-grade, and takes some of the annoyance out of one of the least exciting parts of a tubeless setup.

Do most riders need one? Absolutely not.

Would I happily use one every time I tape a wheel? Yep. That’s the problem with nice tools.

entry.title: Exposure Joystick 19 Gets Mega 33% Output Boost with Same Runtime, in Same Small Size
entry.content:
Exposure once again gives their popular lightweight Joystick helmet light a big upgrade – this time boosting output to 1600 lumens for its 19th generation. On the gunmetal grey anodized outside, it looks exactly the same as the outgoing model – outside of a couple extra cooling fins. But inside, there’s a more powerful LED, the same battery which gets the same burn times, and a reshaped lens for improved peripheral vision when night riding.

Upgraded 2026 Exposure Joystick mk19 1600lm helmet light

Just last fall, Exposure’s long-running and most-popular helmet light – the tiny Joystick – got a pretty significant 18th-generation performance upgrade. That one added hands-free TAP tech to be able to switch modes without searching for a tiny button while riding. You can even set it so you just tap your helmet to change modes. Plus, it added an extra 50lm of light output and a 4% bigger battery to keep the same runtime.

Now, Exposure have an even bigger update for the Joystick mk19.

This time, it gets 400 lumens more, bringing its peak output to 1600lm with an upgraded lens. Typically, the Joystick would often be used as a helmet-mounted light to combine with a bar light for off-road riding. But this big output increase is enough to use it on its own, too – on your head or handlebar – for less intense night riding like gravel or bikepacking.

That’s especially good news, because I’ve found Exposure lights to be extremely high-quality and long-lasting, but they aren’t exactly cheap. Now, one tiny light can double as a helmet light for fast technical mountain bike, but also offer plenty of illumination from your bar for less demanding singletrack or gravel road riding, or even commuting.

And it’s just as small as ever. 112mm long and a max 30mm in diameter at its head. It is again a few grams heavier, now up to 111g to account for a slightly heavier, high-capacity battery tucked inside.

Tech details

  • compact mini flashlight-style cycling headlight
  • CNC-machined 6063 alloy housing with integrated heatsink fins
  • 1600 lumen max output, up 33% from mk18
  • new single white XHP50 Cree LED for bright, clear illumination
  • new dimpled lens design for improved peripheral visibility
  • various helmet, bar, or any GoPro mount compatible with various clip-on holders
  • Action Clip with screw-on Helmet Mount included (with 2 bolt lengths) allows GoPro mount compatibility
  • Security Leash also included
  • bar, cleat, out-front, and braze-on mounts available separately
  • 1-36 hours of runtime in about a dozen different output modes
    (6 sets of modes, with individual High, Medium & Low settings)
  • same 400mAh battery inside
  • 1-button setup & control, with simple 3-color LED indicator on the back of the light
  • TAP tech hands-free adjustment
  • USB-C charging in ~2hrs, can be continuously charged while illuminating from most power banks
  • IP67 waterproofing for use in all weather conditions & IK09 impact rating
  • 111g claimed weight
  • UK-made in West Sussex, England
  • Exposure warranties all lights for 2 years, 3 years if bought direct from their website, LEDs guaranteed for life
  • designed to work for many years, Exposure also services (and can sometimes update) previous-generation lights for much longer

Exposure Joystick 19 – Pricing & availability

The new, higher-output Exposure Joystick 19 sells for $215 / £195 / 195€. That’s exactly the same price as the Joystick 18, which I personally use on my helmet for nighttime trail riding together with a bar light.

I’m really happy with Exposure’s move to their new ‘Helmet Mount with Action Camera Clip’ that allows easy mounting to the top of a helmet, as long as it has a central vent on top. But also the fact that you can take the helmet mount plates off, and bolt it onto any GoPro-style mount, too. I also like the simple rubber band Quick Release Handlebar Mount, which will cost you an extra 15€ to quickly clip it onto a round handlebar.

Get yours now, directly from Exposure’s website or their global retailer network.

ExposureLights.com

entry.title: MET Manta 3 Aero Road Helmet is Already World Championship-Winning, Plus 6W Faster
entry.content:
We already spotted MET’s new Manta 3 aero road helmet on UAE women’s and men’ pro heads in the World Tour this season, from last year’s World Champ Tadej Pogačar to this year’s new champ Brandon McNulty. But now you can buy one. And MET has shared all the tech details about what makes their core road racing helmet faster, and safer, than ever.

MET Manta 3 aero road racing helmet

Last week MET unveiled the more affordable no-carbon Trenta 2 version of their airflow-maxed road helmet. But if speed is your priority on the bike, it’s time to look at the new Manta 3 on the aero road side.

The Manta 3 officially broke cover this season at Milan-Sanremo in March, where Pogačar sprinted to that crash-tattered & bloody win ahead of Tom Pidcock. Not a bad first race for the new MET lid. Did a new aero helmet help him win? It likely didn’t hurt, if MET’s wind tunnel claims are right.

They explain that at the 50km/hr speeds that road racers see, aero drag starts to become a really big obstacle to overcome. So they spent years refining the Manta, and came out saving an extra 6W over the gen 2 helmet with this new design.

Plus – thanks to the revised three main forward-facing vents design, lower-profile MIPS Air Node system inside, revised internal channeling, and a new F1-inspired pair of Double Deck air deflectors at the back – the new Manta 3 promises a 10% improvement in ventilation, as well.

Old vs. New aero shaping

MET describes the new Manta 3 as being a bit shorter and smoother than the Manta 2. That’s especially evident in the shift of its ‘tail’ further back and lower, and fewer sharp edges.

The obvious move from two to three main front vents is visually distinct, of course. But the most significant change is the loss of the top vent, as we’ve seen almost every modern aero helmet remove any edges or openings from the top of all their latest designs to reduce drag.

Tech details

  • wind tunnel-optimized aero road helmet
  • MET ranks it as “the fastest” in benchmark tests in their own “Tube” wind tunnel
  • in-mold EPS construction with full-wrap 3-piece polycarbonate shell
  • MIPS Air Node lightweight anti-rotation protection
  • protection optimized from analysis of 142 real crash-damaged helmets worn by UAE Team Emirates between 2019-2025
  • Coolmax integrated pads
  • two side vents function as sunglasses ports
  • Double Deck rear vent air deflectors
  • dial- & height-adjustable Safe-T Orbital Fit System
  • Air Lite straps with adjustable under-ear hardware
  • Virginia Tech Helmet Lab 5-star safety rating
  • CE | US | AS-NZ safety certifications
  • 3 sizes (S 52-56cm, M 56-58cm & L 58-61cm)
  • 250g claimed weight (CE, size M)

MET Manta 3 – Pricing, options & availability

The new redesigned MET Manta 3 aero road bike helmet sells for $375 / 330€, including a soft helmet bag for storage. It is available now in six relatively low-key colors. Pick from all-black, all-white, white with black logos and EPS, dark grey, light silver, or a red-to-black fade.

MET-hemets.com

entry.title: LOOK Turns the 795 Blade RS 3 Into a 50-Bike Art Edition With Julia Hariri
entry.content:
LOOK is giving its fastest road bike a gallery treatment.

The French brand has teamed up with Berlin-based German-Iranian artist Julia Hariri for the second installment of its The Art of Cycling series, producing just 50 individually numbered 795 Blade RS 3 framesets with Hariri’s artwork worked across the frame.

This isn’t just a custom paint option, either. Each collection includes: a painted 795 Blade RS 3 frame and fork, a LOOK Aeropost 5 carbon seatpost, special-edition Keo Blade Ceramic Ti pedals, a 40 x 60cm fine-art print, and a cotton tote carrying the same graphic language. You can get this slick edition and be the envy of your artist cycling crew for only $6,990 / €6,990 / £6,590. Which really isn’t that bad, considering it can go on the wall whenever you’re ready for a new frame or when road bikes evolve to 32″ wheels.

Julia Hariri Meets the 795 Blade RS 3

Hariri’s work centers heavily on the female form, movement, and autonomy, and that carries directly onto the bike.

LOOK says the collaboration explores what it calls the “female gaze”. Flowing shapes and bold color wrap the 795 Blade RS 3 rather than simply sitting on top as a decorative graphic.

Hariri originally painted three frames by hand.

One frame stays with the artist. One goes into the permanent collection at La Maison LOOK museum in Nevers. The third will support a charity fundraising campaign to expand access to 12 years of free, safe, quality education for girls.

For the production run, LOOK’s design team reworked the artwork individually across all six frame sizes. Running from XXS through XL, rather than scaling one graphic up and down. LOOK says each size was redrawn so the forms keep their proportions and flow across the full range.

Each frame is then individually numbered from 1/50 to 50/50.

The Art of Cycling

This is the second project in LOOK’s The Art of Cycling series. The brand uses it to connect its race-bike engineering with artists outside the traditional cycling world.

LOOK CEO Federico Musi frames the series around something the company has leaned into for decades: performance and aesthetics carrying equal weight.

That philosophy fits LOOK better than most. The brand’s history is full of engineering firsts, from clipless pedals to early carbon race bikes. LOOK has also never been shy about bold graphics, unusual finishes, or bikes that look different from the rest of the peloton.

The Hariri edition pushes that side of the brand much harder.

Keo Blade Ceramic Ti Collector Pedals Included

The package also includes a matching pair of Keo Blade Ceramic Ti pedals decorated with Hariri artwork. They come in a dedicated collector box and use LOOK’s titanium spindle and ceramic-bearing setup.

That’s a nice touch, because a bike this visually specific would look a little unfinished with standard black pedals bolted on.

The included art print is produced on Hahnemühle Photo Matt Fiber paper, while the tote carries Hariri’s custom graphic. LOOK clearly wants this to feel like a complete collection, not a painted frameset with a couple of extras tossed in.

The Art of Cycling x Julia Hariri – Pre-Order Now Open

The LOOK 795 Blade RS 3 The Art of Cycling x Julia Hariri edition goes up for preorder today, November 12, 2026, through LOOK and select dealers. Deliveries are expected to begin in December.

The collection will also debut at Rouleur Live in London, running November 12-14 at The Truman Brewery. Hariri will be on the LOOK stand during the Thursday evening launch for a live painting performance.

At nearly $7000 / 7000€ before drivetrain, wheels, or cockpit, this isn’t exactly the practical choice.

But practical isn’t really the point. Plenty of 795 Blade RS 3s are already built to go fast. Only 50 of them will look like this.

LookCycle.com

entry.title: Van Rysel launches updated RCR-R and RCR-R Pro road bikes with lower weight and improved aerodynamics
entry.content:
Cyclist
Van Rysel launches updated RCR-R and RCR-R Pro road bikes with lower weight and improved aerodynamics

Van Rysel has updated its RCR-R aero/lightweight bike, which it launched in 2024. Decathlon’s performance bike brand says the update is the outcome of two and a half years of development, resulting in an improved mix of aerodynamics, low weight and stable descending.

At a claimed 705g for a size M frame, Van Rysel says that the new RCR-R Pro is the lightest frame it has ever developed. 

It’s aiming high with the new bike, with Van Rysel race product manager Jérémie Debeuf saying, ‘The new RCR-R brings Van Rysel’s ambition to fruition – to design the world’s highest-performing equipment with the aim of securing victory at the Tour de France.’

That project has started well, with Paul Seixas winning Il Lombardia on the new bike last month, become the race’s youngest ever winner in the process. ‘

The bike is lighter, more aerodynamic and, above all, more stable on descents,’ Debeuf says. ‘When you’re travelling at over 100kmh, confidence in your kit is paramount.’

Co-developed with Decathlon CMA CGM pro team

Van Rysel says it used computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to develop 13 prototypes for the new bike, of which five were wind-tunnel-tested. The main changes from the first generation RCR-R appear to be concentrated at the front end, with a deeper head tube and fork legs, which would mirror the changes typically seen in other recent bike updates, such as the S-Works Tarmac SL9.

Van Rysel has also designed a new aero bottle cage, claiming it can save as much as 6.3 watts at 45kmh, with further details to follow. 

The Decathlon CMA CGM pro riders rode the new bike in races and high altitude training in the Spanish Sierra Nevada, helping Van Rysel’s product development team to refine the final design. 

According to Decathlon CMA CGM pro Nicolas Prodhomme, ‘There’s a real improvement in terms of lightness and aerodynamics, but it’s the bike’s overall handling that impresses me most. The bike is responsive when you need to accelerate, whilst offering stability, particularly on fast, technical descents.’

Two frame grades, each in four specs

As with the first generation bike, the top specs of the new RCR-R will be available with the premium Pro frameset, which is made of what Van Rysel describes as ‘a combination of super-high modulus and high-modulus carbon fibre’. 

It claims a 705g frame weight in size M for the RCR-R Pro, with a 360g fork weight – a reduction from the claimed 790g frame and 380g fork of the first generation bike.

The RCR-R Pro will be available with SRAM Red, with a 6.6kg claimed weight, Shimano Dura-Ace, with a 6.9kg weight, and SRAM Force AXS and Shimano Ultegra, both with a 7.1kg claimed weight.

The lower priced non-Pro frameset has a claimed 883g frame weight in size M and is fitted with the same 360g fork as the RCR-R Pro.

Van Rysel will sell the standard RCR-R with SRAM Force AXS, with a 7.5kg claimed weight, Shimano Ultegra (claimed weight 7.4kg), Shimano 105 Di2 (claimed weight 7.8kg) and SRAM Rival AXS (claimed weight 7.9kg).

Euro prices range from €3,299 (approx £2,760) to €8,499 (approx £7,100), with prices in other currencies to follow. That top-spec pricetag is a little lower than the €9,000 price for the flagship RCR-R Pro when it was launched in 2024. The new RCR-R and RCR-R Pro will be available to buy from January 2027 across Europe, the UK and North and South America.

Over the past few seasons, Decathlon’s pro riders have generally chosen to ride the RCR-F Pro aero bike over the previous generation lightweight/allrounder RCR-R Pro, so it will be interesting to see if they now change allegiances to the updated RCR-R Pro.

The post Van Rysel launches updated RCR-R and RCR-R Pro road bikes with lower weight and improved aerodynamics appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: MET launches updated Manta 3 aero helmet, claiming better ventilation and reduced drag
entry.content:
Cyclist
MET launches updated Manta 3 aero helmet, claiming better ventilation and reduced drag

MET has updated its Manta aero race helmet, claiming a 10% improvement in ventilation and a 6-watt reduction in drag. 

The helmet’s aerodynamics are tuned for a rider in an attacking, head-down riding position and MET says the internal channelling has been designed to enhance airflow. 

It reckons the Manta 3 is the fastest aero helmet when it was benchmarked against (unnamed) competitors in an in-house wind-tunnel. 

MET has also switched from MIPS C2 to the lightweight MIPS Air Node Pro rotational impact protection system, where the sliding plane is integrated into the helmet’s Coolmax padding. 

The rear vents have been simplified from the previous generation Manta, switching to two parallel horizontal ribs, which MET says are inspired by the air deflectors used on Formula 1 cars and claims improve aero performance and heat dissipation.

A change to the shape of the outer surface at the rear of the helmet is also said to optimise airflow and the front vents and strap placement have been designed for eyewear compatibility. A full wrap shell aims to increase durability.

Crash-tested by the pros

MET says it has crash tested over 250 Manta 3 helmets as part of the new model’s development, putting them through a total of 745 impact tests in the lab. It also collected 142 crashed helmets from the UAE Team Emirates pro team and compared the effect of real world impacts with its lab testing to help validate its results. 

The helmet has been in use by the pros throughout the 2026 season, starting with Milan-San Remo, where Tadej Pogačar wore it to the win, while Brandon McNulty was wearing the Manta 3 when he won the men’s Road World Championships in Montreal in September. 

MET has sent the new helmet to Virginia Tech’s Helmet Lab for testing, where it was awarded a five star safety rating. 

It claims the Manta 3’s 250g weight in size M, which fits heads from 56 to 58cm, makes it one of the lightest aero helmets on the market and claims its shape is comfortable for a range of different head shapes.

The size S helmet fits heads from 52 to 56cm and has a 240g claimed weight, while the L fits heads from 58 to 61cm and weighs a claimed 280g.

The new MET Manta 3 is on sale immediately, priced at £300 / $375 / €330 and available in six shell/logo colour combinations.

entry.title: Suunto Mostly Leaving Finland, Wahoo Adds Oura/COROS/Apple Sleep Integrations
entry.content:
We’ve got two sports tech news items hitting today, both with a Finnish connection. First up is news about Suunto continuing to dismantle said Finnish connection, and then after that there’s news of Wahoo joining up with Finnish brand Oura, maker of Oura rings.

Suunto Announces Further Finnish Layoffs:

According to an article published this morning by the largest daily newspaper in Finland, Suunto plans to lay off the majority of remaining staff in Finland, and continue consolidating functions in China, via its owners since 2022 – Liesheng. HS (the newspaper) reports that Suunto had 160 people in Finland, and on Monday the company notified 118 of those that their jobs may be lost. Suunto (pre-acquisition) had moved most of its less expensive watch manufacturing to China, and then in 2024 that followed with moving all sports watch manufacturing to China.

Since then, Liesheng has shifted virtually all Suunto software development to China, as well as most other functions. That has resulted in Suunto actually delivering frequent software updates on a predictable quarterly-ish update schedule. While many of these features are mostly catch-up to their competitors, this was a massive change from the previous decade, which saw on-again/off-again progress in terms of making competitive products.

While 2024 and 2025 saw Suunto deliver a number of strong watch contenders at very good prices, since this summer Suunto has taken an oddly different tack – specifically around pricing. They launched the Suunto Run 2 at $349USD, substantially higher than the $249 the previous Suunto Run 1 was launched at (especially given it was originally billed as Suunto’s entry-level/budget watch). This price wasn’t completely a deal-killer given the more premium materials twist. But the real head-scratcher was the recent Suunto Race 3S, which was bafflingly priced at $599USD, a 70% price increase over the previous Suunto Race S unit (it also shifted to more premium materials). All while falling far short of the much less expensive COROS Pace 4 Pro that was launched a week prior. Point being, pricing shifts may be joining workforce shifts.

Having been around Suunto a long-long time, nearly all of the people I knew who had been there for decades are now gone. While Suunto the brand is still making good watches, it’ll soon be pretty hard to meaningfully call it a Finnish brand. Nonetheless, there’s plenty of non-Finnish sports brands still making great GPS watches. Only time will tell whether Suunto, as a brand/name, can stay the course of making good watches, country association aside.

(And as an aside, I was actually wrapping up my written review of the Suunto Run 2, after almost precisely a month of wearing it, when this news hit this morning, so expect that review tomorrow.)

Wahoo Partners with Oura/COROS/Apple Health For Readiness Insights:

Wahoo has joined Zwift in announcing recent integrations with Oura (Zwift did so a week or so ago). Apparently, whoever at Oura is responsible for partner integrations is going for the Christmas bonus this year. This new integration with Wahoo feeds your Oura ring data into their Training Insights feature, allowing you to combine that data with your Wahoo training data.

But Oura isn’t the only one. Both COROS and Apple Health are coming next week. However, Oura is here today, so I’ll show that. First, setting it up is relatively easy. You’ll see a notice at the top that you can connect Oura; simply tap that, and a few seconds later you’re done.

From there on the main dashboard, you’ll see the Recovery Response metric populated. This isn’t a direct metric from Oura, but rather a calculated score by Wahoo.

In this case, if I were to tap that, I’m brought to a different dashboard that shows a bit more of my sleep details, including last night’s sleep, last night’s HRV, and last night’s resting HR. It also shows temperature and respiration rate. For SpO2, I didn’t have that toggled on in the Oura app (it’s a manual toggle). Currently, when I tap on any of the metrics for more details, it shows that a historical chart is coming soon.

For the mental capacity bit, that’s a short game/test you take over 90 seconds, typing when a color square shows up, how many milliseconds it takes you to respond to it. Since I just started that fun today, it takes 3 days of anxiety-inducing tapping to light up that scorecard.

For the specifics, here are some extra tidbits from Wahoo:

Data imported from Oura: HRV (rMSSD), resting heart rate and sleep (time asleep), plus blood oxygen (SpO2), respiratory rate and body temperature as illness markers. Readiness and sleep need are calculated by Wahoo, not imported from Oura. When Recovery Response is elevated, My Readiness flags the anomaly to the athlete.
Integration: One-way, with data flowing from Oura to Wahoo.
Compatibility: All generations of the Oura ring. An active Oura membership is required.
Historical data: When connecting, athletes can import up to 90 days of Oura data, so My Readiness has a personal baseline from day one.
Training history: My Readiness uses every workout in the athlete’s Wahoo App history, whichever device or platform recorded it.

In any case, as for COROS & Apple Health, those are again slated to light up on Tuesday the 17th (November). So I’ll give those a poke then.

With that – thanks for reading!

entry.title: Meet the maker: Ben Spurrier of Condor
entry.content:
Cyclist
Meet the maker: Ben Spurrier of Condor

It doesn’t take much to turn heads at the cafe. A set of deep-section rims or a frame in some colour other than black will usually elicit a few sideways glances. By contrast, in the obscure and esoteric world of custom bicycles, the bar is somewhat higher.

Take a bike show such as Bespoked, where some of the weirdest and most wonderful two-wheeled creations in the world gather under one roof for a few days each year.

Here, only the most beautiful and bizarre bikes stand out. That could be due to some sort of alien geometry, an experimental new construction method or, in the case of Condor’s stunning Porta Romana Italia RC, a particularly decadent paintjob.

Condor is a name that requires little introduction. The London marque has been building bikes since 1948 when Monty Young opened the original shop on Gray’s Inn Road. In the decades that have passed, its frames have been ridden by everyone from club riders to professional racers.

It’s a brand rooted in classic framebuilding and the golden age of metal bikes, but one that refuses to be governed entirely by nostalgia. Aesthetics lean towards the classic – diamond frames and metal tubes prevail across the range – but head of design Ben Spurrier doesn’t shy away from modern details either.

What has changed is where those frames are built. Condor’s production moved from Britain to northern Italy in 2006, and its frames continue to be made there today. And a bike that encapsulates all of the above is the Italia RC, a blisteringly fast alloy race bike with classic lines and a relatively accessible pricetag, despite the fact it is handmade in Veneto.

‘It’s a lightweight frame with racing pedigree for anyone who wants the snappy ride characteristics of a performance machine without the costs of a high-end carbon frame,’ Spurrier explains.

‘Each frame is made by our master craftsmen, one at a time rather than on a production line. This allows a single builder to dedicate greater attention to detail and use less material at each join, ultimately enhancing the overall quality of the ride. We also use custom-drawn 7000-series aluminium, which has an exceptional strength-to-weight ratio that allows for thinner and lighter tubes for a stiff yet durable frame construction.’

The Italia RC was developed alongside Condor’s UCI Continental team, JLT Condor, which at the time was home to the peloton’s tallest rider, Conor Dunne at 6ft 7in, whose gargantuan 64cm R&D model served as the ultimate test in 2016.

‘Conor rode it to a fifth-place finish in the Tour of Taiwan, battling through a challenging mountain-top finish to secure his general classification position,’ says Spurrier. ‘The long alloy tubes proved their strength in competition, their stiffness for elite performance and their ride quality for gruelling all-day breakaways.’

This stunning gilded version of the bike is the result of a collaboration between Condor and Porta Romana, a UK-based interior design and lighting outfit that has done everything from creating installations for the Royal Academy of Arts to dreaming up unique designs for homes, galleries and hotels around the world.

The goal was to help support Clerkenwheels’ fundraising adventure ride, which saw podcasters Jonathan Forster and Tom Bourne ride 430km from Plymouth to Clerkenwell to raise money for United in Design, a charity devoted to creating opportunities for underrepresented talent in the design industry. The one-of-a-kind bike was then raffled off at Clerkenwell Design Week, with all proceeds going to UiD.

Flying colours

Porta Romana’s painting studio is central to the design process. It’s there that they have spent more than three decades building on the craft of hand-painted finishes, developing their own unique library. Each patination takes a skilled team weeks to develop, sampling layer upon layer of colour in search of the perfect Porta Romana finish.

‘Using their extensive paint library, I created the design using their Burnt Ochre finish and asked them to gild the Condor logo, head tube and fork,’ explains Spurrier.

‘The finish is applied by hand using proprietary techniques to build up layers of paint to achieve the final depth and texture. On top of that, the logos, details and fork internals are all gilded by hand using gold leaf.’

If the finish alone isn’t enough to grab your attention, the all-Italian components might do the trick. The bike is fitted with a full Campagnolo Super Record wireless groupset and matching Campagnolo Shamal wheels – a decision, Spurrier says, that was made to attract as much attention for the ride and the charity as possible. For those who like what they see enough to open their wallets, the good news is that a Campag-dripping Italia RC can be yours for £7,200. As for the finish, that’s harder to put a pricetag on, but Spurrier’s best guess puts it around £1,500 for the full Porta Romana treatment.

• Condor Italia RC, £7,200, Porta Romana build approx £8,700. Visit condorcycles.com for more information
