entry.title: Sturdy Cycles Launches Two New Cnc-Machined, Uk-Made Titanium Bikes: Fosse for Road and Drove for Gravel
entry.content:
Somerset-based titanium bicycle maker Sturdy Cycles is launching two bike models at Rouleur Live in London on 12 November: Fosse, for the road, and Drove, for gravel.

Sturdy Cycles Fosse and Drove Quick Hits

  • Prices
    • Fosse frame kit £6,000 (inc UK VAT) / £5,000 ex VAT
    • Add a SRAM Force Groupset and full build kit from £4,511.60 (inc UK VAT) / £3,759.67 ex VAT
    • Drove frame kit £6,000 (inc UK VAT) / £5,000 ex VAT
    • Add a SRAM Force groupset and full build kit £4,137.60 (inc UK VAT) / £3,448 ex VAT
    • Frame kit and build kit together make a complete bike, from £10,511.60 (Fosse) and £10,137.60 (Drove) inc UK VAT. Details and upgrade option below.
  • Headset: Enduro stainless steel, lifetime warranty – included
  • Bottom bracket: T47-68 (68mm wide T47 threaded shell)
  • Rear axle: 142×12mm; titanium thru axle included (167mm long, M12×1mm thread)
  • Derailleur hanger: UDH; titanium Sturdy edition with phosphor-bronze threads – included
  • Brake mount: Adjustable for 140mm or 160mm rotors at the frame (fork: Fosse 140mm or 160mm, Drove 160mm or 180mm)
  • Seatpost: Aero profile titanium seatpost machined in-house – included
  • Stem: Titanium, machined in-house – included
  • Fork: Fosse: ENVE IN-Route Road, 370mm design length. Drove: ENVE IN-Route Gravel, 395mm design length, with cargo mounts – included
  • Cable routing: Through the headset. Electronic groupsets only (SRAM, Shimano and Campagnolo). Wire exit points for Shimano added if required
  • Bosses:
    • Fosse: 2 bottle cage mounts in the front triangle and mudguard mounts.
    • Drove: 2 bottle cage mounts in the front triangle, a 3rd under the down tube, top tube bag mounts, and mudguard mounts
  • Tire clearance: Fosse: 35mm maximum recommended measured tire width on a 700c rim (frame 38mm, ENVE fork 35mm). Drove: 50mm (frame 55mm, ENVE fork 50mm)

Overview

The frames are built from drawn titanium tubes joined to CNC-machined titanium parts, machined, welded and finished at the workshop in Frome. Every frame kit includes an ENVE IN-Route carbon fork, a titanium seatpost and stem machined in-house, an Enduro headset, a titanium rear thru axle, a titanium UDH hanger with phosphor-bronze inserts and titanium bottle boss bolts.

The bikes showcase the latest engineering and manufacturing developments from the workshop: the 3D-printed junctions and components of earlier Sturdy frames have been replaced by fully redesigned, CNC-machined titanium parts. Every frame is designed, engineered, machined, fabricated and finished by hand at the Sturdy Cycles workshop in Frome, Somerset. The new manufacturing approach introduces a sharp, modern yet minimal aerodynamic aesthetic, ensuring every Sturdy remains a unique proposition: truly functional UK engineering refined with handmade finesse.

Both bikes come in six sizes, each in three stack heights (Low, Medium and Tall), so each model offers 18 fits. The versatile sizing is designed to streamline fabrication whilst still offering riders much of the fit of a custom frame. The Sturdy website features a new suite of interactive tools designed to help customers find their perfect fit, compare their existing bike against the new models and even design their own custom Cerakote finish.

Fosse

Fosse is a highly versatile titanium road bike. Its three stack heights let riders fine-tune the fit for speed, but its core focus is longer, endurance-friendly riding. A relatively low bottom bracket offsets the wider tires now common on road builds, keeping the bike stable at speed without losing the agility expected of a road bike. With the included ENVE IN-Route Road carbon fork, it accommodates tires up to 700×35mm.

Fosse Way: the Roman road that ran from Exeter to Lincoln, built in the first century AD. It still cuts an almost straight line across Somerset, a few miles from the Frome workshop.

Drove

Drove is a modern gravel bike for going further off the beaten track, shaped by years of designing, building and riding bikes across the wet byways, bridleways and holloways of Somerset and Wiltshire. Longer chainstays give stability at speed and sure-footed traction on steep, loose climbs; balanced front-end geometry tracks straight over rough ground. With the included ENVE IN-Route Gravel carbon fork, it takes tires up to 700×50mm, and adds a third bottle mount, top tube bag mounts and mudguard mounts.

Drove, or drovers’ roads: ancient rural routes once used to move livestock. Many are of unknown age and some date back to medieval times. These rough tracks criss-cross the Somerset and Wiltshire landscape.

Built To Last

Road grime, grit and water find their way into everything, so both frames have phosphor-bronze threads and bushes at the thru-axles and seatpost clamp, the places where titanium has a habit of seizing. Each frame kit includes an Enduro stainless steel headset with a lifetime bearing warranty, and the frames are covered by a lifetime warranty for the original owner. An interchangeable rear disc brake caliper mount swaps between 140mm and 160mm rotors without an adapter.

Finding the right fit

Sturdy’s online fitting tools help riders choose between the 18 fits. The size selector works from the position of the bike they ride now, the bar position calculator finds where their bars sit today, and compare geometry draws any two frames over each other, or over their current bike.

Finish

Every frame, stem and seatpost has a shot-peened raw titanium finish. The standard finish, included in the price, adds a down tube logo, oversize or small, in brushed titanium or one of nine Cerakote colors. Riders who want something more personal can choose a custom theme (£720 inc UK VAT / £600 ex VAT), a one or two-color Cerakote design, or a bespoke finish (from £2,400 inc UK VAT / £2,000 ex VAT). Details are agreed with each customer after ordering.

Cerakote is a highly durable ceramic-based coating, best known in the firearms industry. Its toughness and scratch resistance make it well suited to a bike that will be ridden hard all year round.

Customers can try every option on the frame in Sturdy’s online finishing selector, and see examples of past custom finishes in the past builds gallery.

Made In The UK And Available To Order Now

Each frame kit is made to order, with a lead time of about six weeks. The first frames will be dispatched in Nov/Dec 2026. Once a customer has placed an order, Tom and Jack begin the manufacturing process, and the customer confirms their fit and finish details through a personal build page.

The Frome workshop uses CNC machining to make and finish the frame’s machined titanium parts, combined with manual machining and traditional hand tools to ensure every frame meets Sturdy’s standards. All Sturdy Cycles frames are prepared, welded, and finished by hand under one roof. The workshop hosts a range of professional finishing equipment, including parts tumbling, polishing, glass bead blasting and wet spray painting using Cerakote ceramic coatings. Sturdy Cycles is proud to be one of the only UK titanium bicycle manufacturers physically manufacturing, finishing, and assembling everything it produces in-house. Workshop visits can be arranged for customers and press, and international shipping is available.

Coming in 2027

A Sturdy titanium fork for each model is due in 2027, raising tire clearance to 38mm on Fosse and 55mm on Drove.

Find out all the details and more at Sturdy Cycles.

The post Sturdy Cycles Launches Two New Cnc-Machined, Uk-Made Titanium Bikes: Fosse for Road and Drove for Gravel appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: 2026 Sedona Mountain Bike Festival: Finally Fall – Spencer Harding
entry.content:
Spencer rolled upstate this past weekend for the first Fall iteration of the Sedona Mountain Bike Festival in…well, Sedona! This was the event’s first Fall seasonal festival, a switch from Spring after many years of unfortunate weather. The weather was perfect, and Spencer found some sweet brands and bits to highlight. See what he found below…

Sedona Mountain Bike Festival

The Sedona Mountain Bike Festival feels more like the bike-demo portion of the now-defunct Interbike than a larger trade show like Sea Otter. The experience really does cater to allowing attendees to ride bikes, try on clothes, and put their hands on products they have seen on the internet. It is a very tactile experience, and as such, I have a whole separate post focusing on actually riding some bikes instead of just shooting pretty photos of them.

Fear not, I also have a whole section in this article focusing on some beautiful builds from the festival.

From Spring to Fall

In the past, Sedona Mountain Bike Festival was hosted in the spring. After a few years of snow and rain that made riding difficult or nearly impossible, the festival owners moved the event to the Fall. With spring peppered with bike and gear releases ahead of Sea Otter, many companies kept their releases close to their chest before the big trade show.

Free from the clutches of product release cycles, Sedona MTB Fest feels like it can stand on its own legs and focus on what it does best: get people out riding in a gorgeous place. The festival offers group rides, shuttles all over Sedona, clinics, classes, and any other permutation you can imagine to give people an excuse to get out of the festival grounds and onto some red dirt.

After the initial 9 am “Running of the Dads” to get in line for precious demo slots, the festival calms down for a few hours. It is a very hurry-up-and-wait situation for all the brave souls managing the bike fleets. I have only ever seen such a line of eager riders forming well before opening at one festival, Sedona.

Twisted Spoke CBD

My curiosity was initially caught by Twisted Spoke’s CBD chamois cream offering, which seems as novel as it could be useful. I was really in the market for some sleepy time supplements and snagged a jar of CBN softgels to replace my usual THC and CBN gummies. Gabe had a plethora of gummies, tinctures, and even sparkling waters with more permutations of acronyms than one could imagine. I’m looking forward to sleeping well with these tablets after the festival.

Adidas 5.10

Adidas is finally leaning into fully rebadging the 5.10 lineup with the triple stripes. As seen above, they have the new Slueth Pro, Freerider Pro Boa, and Freerider Clip coming at various times in 2027.

Also, the much-lauded Guide Tennie is back!

Rogue Panda

The Pandas have been busy up in Flagstaff this past year. With the latest release of their new Double Track mounting system, Rogue Panda once again shows their dedication to constantly pushing bag technology forward. The Double Track system uses two carbon poles and TPU spacers for a more secure and robust mounting system for their custom frame bags. They also had their two new rack-top bags: the Elden rack-top harness and Picket Post. The rear rack also showcased their Buckskin mini panniers, which use the Old Man Mountain Flip mounting system. Add in their redesigned Blue Ridge Handlebar Harness V2 and Rogue Panda has every bag you could need for your dream setup in all kinds of amazing fabrics, patterns, and colors.

Velo In A Jar

Ava of Velo in a Jar had a humble booth, featuring recycled jewelry made from bike tubes, beer cans, and even clock parts. She had a menagerie of great gifts. Her work offered a cozy respite from the downhill bro aesthetic of many booths.

Cognative MTB

I love a snap-button shirt, so the Cognative MTB technical flannel caught my eye. With plenty of thoughtful details and technical fabrics that didn’t feel overly plasticky, the flannel felt nice in hand. You really can’t beat grabbing a fistful of shirts and ripping open snap buttons to air out on a long climb.

All Over Apparel

Salida-based All Over had a small but lovely lineup of clothes on show at the fest. With the main focus and name seemingly a play on overalls, All Over offers a technical stretch-fabric iteration of the classic. While the overalls look quite fun, it is almost always too hot for such fashion in Tucson, so I opted to snag a waffle tee that was oh so soooooft.

Rackspotting at Sedona MTB Fest

Rackspotting at Sedona MTB Fest wasn’t nearly the whole gallery level as the rackspotting at MADE. I found a few gems hidden between all the Stumpjumpers and Trail Cats, including one of the gnarliest derailleurs I’ve ever seen that probably still works…

High Country Adaptive Sports

While out on a test ride, I was lucky enough to catch a group of riders seated in Bowhead adaptive mountain bikes alongside some guides from High Country Adaptive Sports. They offer year-round adaptive programming and recreation opportunities across the Arizona high country.

Beautiful Bicycles of Sedona MTB Fest

I was able to fish out a few beautiful builds from the stalls at the festival. While many companies solely had demo bikes, a few brands- well, just Reeb and Revel- had some gorgeous bikes that warranted a closer look, Radavist style.

Reeb SST Prototype

Reeb showed an updated version of their short-travel steel full-suspension bike, the SST, at the Sedona MTB Festival. While the details weren’t official yet, a few leaked out. Adjusting for yearly geometry inflation, the new SST will have a slightly slacker headtube and a slightly steeper seat tube, around .5º, I was told, for both. The new SST will also feature a butted top tube instead of straight gauge. The bearing will now be removable via collet to make service easier for the home mechanics. The SST will feature revised kinematics, though I don’t have more detail than that. Saving the best for last, 10 mm more stack height across sizes, hell yeah. This bike looks sweeter than ever, and all the improvements make this bike a banger.

Devon’s Custom Reeb Dirt Jumper

Devon is the marketing manager over at I9, and when he helped Reeb out with many days of unpaid labor to help them with bike demos over the past few years, they decided to repay him with this sweet custom Dirt Jumper. Don’t be fooled; Devon is a tall glass of water, and this custom geo was definitely a necessity for someone of his stature. The DJ is dripping in gold I9 bits and topped off with some sparkly labeled Schwable tires, oooohweeeeee.

Revel El Grande Jefe

Revel recently announced their foray into the 32er world with their updated El Jefe titanium hardtail, aptly named El Grande Jefe. With one of the more elegant seat tube bends and a helluva head tube, this hardtail was looking amazing at the show. While this was a rideable prototype, I’m saving myself for a proper ride when production forks become available in the next few months; stay tuned for a full review of the El Grande Jefe soon…

Revel Ti Ranger

Whooooooweee, was this thing a looker. The Ti Ranger was announced just recently, and the initial run of 10 frames sold out in 2 hours. What was expected to just be a fun side project has really caught people’s attention. The combination of a metal, especially titanium, front triangle and Revel’s highly regarded CBF carbon rear triangle is truly stunning. Pulling from all of Revel’s expertise in carbon and titanium, the Ti Ranger is a perfect showpiece to completely encapsulate the brand. Unlike the El Grande Jefe, I did take this for a quick spin; see my Speed Dating article today on the site for some ride details.

Wrap Up

Ok there was a quick downpour on the day at the festival, so it wasn’t perfect weather, but that storm did present a double rainbow afterward with minimal wetting of the trails. I had as lovely a time strolling the aisles as I did getting out on the trails right by the festival grounds and farther around Sedona. With trails available right out of the gate, you couldn’t ask for a more beautiful and apt place to ride a mountain bike than Sedona. I’m already looking forward to 2027…

Please check out my speed-dating bike demos article for a few quick first-ride reviews from the festival!

The post 2026 Sedona Mountain Bike Festival: Finally Fall appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: 2026 Sedona Mountain Bike Festival: Speed Dating Bike Demos From ASYM, Canfield, Spot, Revel, and Trek – Spencer Harding
entry.content:
While cruising the aisle at Sedona Mountain Bike Festival can be its own vortex, escaping the vortex on a sweet demo bike is a treat. Spencer was able to sneak in rides on five unique bikes that caught his eye during his time at Sedona Mountain Bike Festival. See his quick thoughts on bikes from ASYM, Canfield, Revel, Spot, and Trek below…

In past years at Sedona Mountain Bike Festival, I got out for maybe one demo bike at best, either due to weather or time constraints. Flying solo to the weekend for the first time this year, I carved out some time to actually ride.

Each bike was ridden on the same-ish five-mile lap near the Posse Grounds consisting of Grand Central and Adobe Jack trails, with a pedal up the road to access those trails. The paved climb gave insights into pedaling behavior, and the trails had a bit of everything: short drops, steep climbs, berms, tight corners, and rocky ledges. You can only tell so much from an hour-long pedal, but that is why I’m calling it speed dating. I had an hour to let these sweet rides seduce me and wow me.

ASYM Prototype

The prototype fleet from Boulder-based ASYM was a head-turner all weekend at the show. Robb had a handful of rideable prototypes on hand and reached out before the festival to see if I wanted to go for a ride. While the design and aesthetics are polarizing, my curiosity was piqued. As I continue to die on the hill, screaming “stack height is too low” into the wind, how could I ignore Robb’s solution to stack height inequity?

Essentially, ASYM bikes decouple stack height and reach from overall frame size and wheelbase. This allows for someone who would need an XL fit to ride a smaller, say, medium, wheelbase. ASYM bikes achieve this through a linkage bonded to the head tube of the bike, giving the frame greater reach and stack measurement while not sizing up the overall frame size.

I know a loooooot of people will say, just put a longer stem on it; what’s the big deal? Maintaining the familiar feel of a shorter stem and wide bars keeps the bike from the unwanted steering characteristics of a long stem. All the extra effort of bonding the second head tube and engineering the linkage that makes the ASYM bike work can feel overengineered just to avoid a long stem. While that could be true, I believe ASYM’s design opens a new conversation in bike fit and geometry where we can isolate certain measurements and have greater control over bike fit.

I took one of the prototypes on the same loop as every production bike on this list, and out of the gate I was so impressed with the linkage Robb has designed. The linkage had zero, and I mean zero, slop in the mechanism. It was smooth as butter, and if you didn’t look down, you would be unaware of all the engineering behind your bars. The 800+mm stack was instantly a treat, and I felt vindicated in my yelling from the hill I’ve been dying on. The bike rode impressively well considering how odd the front end looked. I never felt like I was going over the bars or had an issue controlling the bike.

I quickly thought of how many people bemoan 29-in wheels vs. 26-in for handling and playfulness. One could have the playful wheelbase of a smaller bike and the fit for however long, tall, or large you may be. My second thought was folks with back issues, as the ASYM mechanism adds so much stack height over a traditional bike. This could help people avoid sketchy stem extenders or excessive stems not rated for trail use.

Robb is passionate about his design and the benefits it can afford the right rider. I loved the extra stack height, and despite how visually odd the whole bike looked, the ride was both comfortable and capable. Reach out to him if you have any questions or might be interested in an ASYM for yourself!

This one was a double date with Robb and a few of his fleet. Things are developing slowly, but I’d be interested in a second date, given the passion behind the engineering.

Canfield Tilt V3 

  • 141 mm rear travel, 140 mm fork travel
  • Adjustable rear travel via shock stroke
    • 210×52.5 mm: 135 mm
    • 210×50 mm: 128 mm
    • 210×55 mm: 141 mm (as ridden)
  • Three chainstay positions (427 / 435 / 442 mm)
  • Recommended fork: 130–150 mm (optimized around 140 mm)
  • Patented Canfield Balance Formula™ (CBF™) suspension
  • 7005 aluminum frame with CNC 7075 T6 links

The Canfield Tilt V3 was the most versatile bike I pedaled over the weekend, with adjustable chainstay lengths and adaptability for three shock strokes to adjust travel. I was curious to try a Canfield Balance Formula-equipped bike that was not carbon for my first time trying the Formula. I love aluminum, and as such, I find myself drawn to the thick welds and industrial aesthetic of the Canfields. While the Brat green color was striking, I love that Canfield offers their bikes in raw aluminum, the best way to let aluminum show off.

The Tilt V3 pedaled as efficiently as the CBF formula promises and delivers equal plush suspension when you point it downhill. Even being a mid-travel aluminum bike with metal wheels, the bike was lively and decidedly non-puggy. Being a demo, it had a bit too much seatpost and a depressing lack of stack height for an XL frame. I would go on a second date with the Canfield Tilt V3 if it had a 210×50 mm shock, 50 mm riser bars, and a raw frame.

Revel Ranger Ti

  • 120 mm rear travel, 130 mm fork travel
  • Titanium front triangle
  • Carbon rear triangle and linkage
  • Shared geometry and kinematics with Ranger V3 Carbon

The belle of the ball for the weekend! Everyone had eyes for this stunning mix of titanium and carbon. Pulling together all the material expertise Revel has accumulated over the years into a singular bike is as impressive as it is expensive. Though I heard they have been selling quite well…

After my first foray with the CBF kinematics on the Canfield, I got to sample Revel’s version of the Formula. I would need to spend more time to develop a more nuanced take on the differences between each brand’s implementations of the system. The Ranger pedals with a calm demeanor and delivers plush suspension on the downhill. Revel only had a size large at the event, and seeing as I doubt this will be available for review, I took my chance, ill-fitting as it was.

The Ti Ranger is for the connoisseur of short travel trail bikes. For a rider who can appreciate the elegant flex of a titanium frame, one who prefers jazz-lines over plowing. Had I a million dollars (~$6k for a frame) and a fine bottle of zinfandel, I would take the Revel Ranger Ti on a second date, but it would need some platforms to be a proper XL frame. A second date would be nice.

Spot Diggity 125

  • 125 mm rear travel, 130 mm fork travel
  • Carbon frame
  • Living Link Titanium plate lower linkage

Hot diggity dog, I was excited to throw my leg over the refined Living Link-equipped diggity. I had a really fun time riding the poppiest of the poppy, Spot Ryve, a few years ago. The titanium plate lower link of the Living Link system provides active energy return on compression, giving Spot bikes a lively, active suspension feel.

Out of the gate, I have to say that I believe the Diggity climbed even better than either of the CBF bikes I rode over the weekend. They all were very, very impressive, but the Diggity squeaked ahead in the climbing department. Finally getting to ride a proper XL after a slew of large frames, presented adequate (it’s never enough) stack and reach to stretch out briefly. I have found Spot bikes to be very dependent on rebound adjustment due to the Living Link suspension. Initially, the bike felt harsh on square impacts, but a quick 2 clicks on the rebound adjustment and the Diggity was feeling almost as plush as the Revel Ranger Ti.

I had a lovely date with the Diggity, and it was the bike I felt most endeared to throughout the weekend. The newer suspension layout is more mild-mannered than the Ryve, in a good way; I pedaled a few years ago. I had such a lovely time with the Diggity that I don’t feel like I would need a second date, likewise in a good way.

Trek Superfly 32

  • 110 mm rear travel, 120 mm fork travel
  • 32″ wheels, ZOMG
  • Carbon frame
  • Details about the frame and components are unreleased

While the Revel Ranger Ti was the belle of the ball, the Trek Superfly prototype was the bike everyone wanted to dance with over the weekend. I secured a reservation first thing Sunday morning before I had to head home. I was glad to have a full 32″, full-suspension experience as my last bike for the weekend, so it would not taint my experience of the other lesser-wheeled-diameter bikes. Details were scarce and embargoed on the new Superfly. The suspension bears the mark of Fox’s RAD (Racing Application Development), signifying the bit’s prototype nature.

My curiosity about the Superfly was the feasibility of a full-suspension 32″ platform rather than the specimen itself. I have no need for, nor a proper opinion on, a world-class XC rig when all is said and done, but being 6’1″, I have to be intrigued by the prospect of a proportional XC bike. Trek only had a large frame, but due to the 32″ wheels and despite the negative rise stem, which I hate with the fiery passion of a thousand suns for taking away the prospect of proper stack height, it was actually fairly comfortable.

As far as I can tell, the geo and fork offsets remain similar to 29″ counterparts and thus feel familiar overall. The Superfly was noticeably smoother through chunder and dodged hangups in rock gardens better than any of the 29″ bikes I pedaled. Riding 32″ Aspens feels like riding 29+ Chronicles at the inception of the last large wheel revolution, in the worst way. Them Aspens do go fast, and I found myself scrubbing speed many times where I had simply coasted by on other bikes. I was likewise unencumbered on tight climbs and descents by the larger wheels.

No one needs to run out and buy a 32″ bike, but if you are already in the market for an XC bike in the future and you happen to be tall, I don’t see any reason to fight the new wheel size. I had far more fun on our date than I would have expected, a wonderful way to cap off a fun weekend of speed dating. I won’t be having a second date with a Trek Superfly, but I do look forward to meeting its other 32″ cousins in the future…

The post 2026 Sedona Mountain Bike Festival: Speed Dating Bike Demos From ASYM, Canfield, Spot, Revel, and Trek appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Classic UK climb: Bealach Ratagan
entry.content:
Cyclist
Classic UK climb: Bealach Ratagan

Little connects Scotland to Spain – not the food, not the weather and definitely not the footballing prowess. However, if you head up to the northwest of Scotland, just inland from the Isle of Skye, you’ll find a 300-year-old connection between Caledonia and Iberia around Loch Duich.

After the Jacobite uprising in 1715, international support was needed for the Scots to restore a Catholic monarchy. Spain became unlikely allies, and an armada of support sailed from southern Europe to the mouth of Loch Duich, where they waited to ignite the third coup.

The call came in June 1719, and two Spanish frigates sailed down the loch, with Jacobite earls, 300 Spaniards and thousands of arms on board. The Highlanders and Spaniards took position at the pass of Glen Shiel, but opposing government forces soon arrived and drove the rebel coalition out. The troops dispersed, the Scottish generals retired to the Western Isles and the Spanish surrendered themselves as prisoners of war.

Despite extinguishing the ill-fated uprising, the government of George I sought to improve the network of defensive roads through the West Highlands. Naturally Glen Shiel was quick to receive this treatment and a route was forged from Shiel Bridge to a brow on the loch’s southern side. That climb would earn the name Bealach Ratagan, a pass that totals 4.5km at an average gradient of 8%. That might not sound like a leg-breaker to some, but it was certainly enough to send those troops running for the hills.

Scotland’s Spanish climb

Bealach Ratagan begins in Shiel Bridge, where the Old Military Road splits from the A87 carrying tourists up the coast to Skye. Beginning at sea level, the opening kilometre is tame at a shallow 2% gradient. It barely rises here, but the road is narrow and passage is rewarded by a broad glimpse to the right across Loch Duich. If the weather plays ball, you’ll spot the heights of the Munros towering on the loch’s northern side. If misty, it’ll make for a wispy lookout across the water.

Keep an eye on the surface too. The famed Nessie hunter Dr McRae claimed to have spotted a Loch Ness-like monster here in the 1930s, although the creature on the recording looks more like a floating hockey stick than a Cretaceous beast. Still, the climb makes a gentle turn inland once you pass a welcome sign to Ratagan, the village to which the climb owes its name. Immediately the slopes begin to bite after the gentle 1.2km introduction.

Article continues below…

Stubborn gradient

The road remains stubborn for the next kilometre at gradients consistently between 6% and 8%. If needed, passing points offer space to weave across to ease the strain, but the gradient persists as the road gently curves around a waterfall nestled among a bush of bracken.

As you turn inland, the hillside now appears to almost be sliced in two: bare below, densely forested with pine above. Beyond halfway the road enters a darker upper section, trading shortbread-tin loch views for damp, tree-lined surroundings.

The gradient also ramps up, and after 2.4km double-digit pitches are the norm, with the metres ticking slowly upwards through the trees. Among the pines, the road eventually widens into an S-bend, where a road sign warns of a 15% gradient. That’s slightly deceiving though, given the slopes have levelled out to a more achievable 10% by this point, just as the road turns toward the loch once again, making for a momentary false flat.

Enjoy it while it lasts, however, because this climb gets particularly nasty in its final kilometre, which arrives once you pass by the car park viewpoint on the road’s water-facing side. In fact, the final thousand metres are at an average gradient of 13%, making this the toughest part of the climb by far. Worse, that average conceals a short pitch at over 22% just as the trees start to thin out.

Thankfully the slopes relent ever so slightly in the final 300m, just as the road shimmies toward the crest. The summit arrives with nothing to mark it other than a chance to look over your shoulder at the view across the loch towards the Five Sisters of Kintail, a chain of peaks rising above 800m.

The landscape feels barely altered since the Battle of Glen Shiel. Who knows, perhaps this was the last view of freedom the Spanish soldiers had before their surrender. For a 21st-century cyclist, at least, there’s a much happier ending to be had here.

The stats

Location Scottish Highlands
Length 4.5km
Summit height 347m
Ascent 335m
Average gradient 8%
Maximum gradient 22.5%
Current best Strava time
KoM Andrew Feather, UK, 12min 25sec
QoM Charlotte Beaton, UK, 17min 21sec

The post Classic UK climb: Bealach Ratagan appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Scarab Cycles Paramo 32er
entry.content:
Santiago Toro, founder of Scarab Cycles, sent us a cool story about the Colombian brand’s first spin at building a 32er out of their Paramo gravel platform. Read on for Santiago’s thesis on how the brand solved a few issues with the new wheel size…

Earlier this year, we had an interesting customer approach us with the idea of building him a 32″ gravel bike. We said yes to exploring the project right away. Why? He had clear arguments and goals for this bike. He knew what he wanted from it and where he expected the 32″ wheels to improve his riding experience. That gave us a reason to start designing.

Rationale Decisions

A Scarab with 32″ wheels? Yes. This is our first. We didn’t want to do one just because of the hype. We wanted to do one because it answered a specific rider’s needs. That rider is Jorge from Ecuador.

Jorge has been riding and racing bikes his whole life. He has a soft spot for everything related to the “unpaved.” He has competed in many MTB races in the high and rough Andes of Ecuador, where technical skill and fitness are pushed to the max. He’s won many times in his category. Clearly, Jorge knows what he wants. And we want to make that happen.

His brief: “I want a gravel bike that I can use to roll through stuff. Something that can keep speed on rough terrain while holding an aggressive gravel position, rather than an MTB-style one. I spend most of my time riding off pavement and only use it to connect sections. I need this to be fast!”

I explained to Jorge that I had been waiting for the right opportunity to build our first 32″ bike. And what better opportunity than to use our Páramo base model as the starting point?

Versatile Geometry

Over the years, we’ve had the chance to work with many Páramo users and adapt the model to their very specific needs: riding terrain, capabilities such as touring, rider size, tire sizes, etc. We’ve learned that each rider has their own way of interpreting riding and that our job is to create a bike that handles the way they envision it.

A gravel bike can be tweaked by changing aspects of its geometry and setup, such as trail, chainstay length, front-center length, wheelbase, stem length, weight distribution, and many more. The complex thing is that they all work in synchrony. One affects the other, and they can’t be fully isolated. But the MASSIVE changes we’ve found over the years come with wheel size and tire size. Those really change how a bike feels.

And to be clear, we don’t believe that bigger wheels or tires make a better bike. First, show me the rider, then how they ride and what they want to achieve with it. Then we define a tire and wheel size that delivers and fits.

Our custom process gives us the flexibility to change a lot. The design process tells us what we should change, what we should preserve, and why.

The Páramo Platform

This iteration of the model felt exactly right. Páramo has gone through years of experimentation and evolution: sliding dropouts, big tire clearance on the Ultra (700 × 58), suspension forks, and, of course, MANY 650B vs. 700C debates, including testing the same bike with both wheelsets.

That experience gave us a starting point for Jorge’s project. His brief brought two priorities together: carrying speed through rough terrain and keeping an aggressive gravel position. The larger wheels were worth exploring, but their diameter alone wouldn’t resolve the brief. We had to design the bike around them and around Jorge.

Dial in the right geometry for Jorge and select the materials to make this Páramo still be a Páramo: a gravel bike designed around his position and intended handling, with the larger wheels working as part of the whole.

We couldn’t simply add clearance and call it done. The wheel size had to be considered alongside the frame dimensions, steering geometry, rider position, and material selection.

Chainstays, seatstays, the down tube, and the top tube had to be specifically sourced to achieve the required lengths, wall thicknesses, and diameters. Longer tubes were part of the solution, but length wasn’t the only criterion. We also had to consider how those tubes would work together.

From Frame to Fork

The real challenge was the fork. Jorge wanted integrated cable routing, and we wanted a fork designed specifically for this gravel bike. Wheel clearance was only one requirement. Its dimensions and offset also had to work with the frame geometry and Jorge’s riding position. A rigid 29er fork wasn’t automatically the right answer just because it could accommodate a large wheel.

The result: a steel fork crafted to meet the specific requirements of this 32″ gravel bike, with integrated cable routing to match the frame’s cable management. We loved working out the design of this steel fork. The Páramo 32″ can now be requested with it, as well as the now-available Zero Components carbon fork designed specifically for 32″ gravel bikes. As with Jorge’s project, the starting point is the rider and what they want the bike to do.

The project included several special parts to match the riding concept.

  • Wheelset: Astral Wanderlust 32″ wheels
  • Groupset: SRAM Red AXS / mullet setup
  • Cockpit: Enve In-Route stem and handlebar, paired with a Thomson titanium seatpost

For us, the point of this project was to bring Jorge’s brief into a coherent design. The wheels, geometry, tubes, fork, and riding position all had to answer the same set of goals. Our manufacturing flexibility gave us room to find that solution. Jorge’s intended use gave us the criteria to make the decisions.

See more at Scarab Cycle’s Blog.

 

The post Scarab Cycles Paramo 32er appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Ruta del Jefe Returns to Arizona’s Sky Islands in April 2027
entry.content:
Ruta del Jefe Returns to Arizona’s Sky Islands in April 2027. This is more than just a gravel ride; it is five cycling routes, four days of community, and a $100,000 fundraising goal that bring a distinctive approach to adventure cycling in the Arizona-Sonora Borderlands.

Ruta del Jefe 2027

Ruta del Jefe returns to the rugged landscapes of southern Arizona April 1–4, 2027, inviting cyclists to explore the Sky Islands through a four-day gathering that combines challenging gravel and adventure riding with education, community, and collective impact.

Held in Patagonia, Arizona, Ruta del Jefe offers five Saturday routes ranging from approximately 30 to 78 miles, with options spanning approachable gravel rides to demanding backcountry adventures featuring thousands of feet of climbing.

But the experience extends well beyond the routes.

Founded by adventure cyclist and route developer Sarah Swallow, Ruta del Jefe brings riders together to learn about the people, cultures, ecosystems, and challenges that shape the Arizona-Sonora Borderlands.

“Adventure cycling gives us an incredible opportunity to connect with the landscapes we travel through,” says Swallow. “Ruta del Jefe asks what happens when we take that connection further, when we get curious about the people who live there, learn about the challenges facing the region, and find ways to contribute.”

Five Routes Through the Sky Islands

The 2027 event features five supported ride options:

  • El Jefe: 78 miles, approximately 6,000 feet of climbing. A challenging adventure route.
  • Sombra: 68 miles, approximately 4,447 feet of climbing. A demanding gravel-plus experience.
  • Cinco: 55 miles, approximately 4,969 feet of climbing. A rugged adventure route.
  • O:Shad: 45 miles, approximately 3,289 feet of climbing. A shorter gravel-plus option.
  • Adela: 30 miles, approximately 1,859 feet of climbing. A more approachable gravel route.

Participants will encounter the region’s characteristic mix of remote roads, rugged mountains, grasslands, and expansive Borderlands scenery.

Additional community rides, workshops, and educational activities take place throughout the four-day gathering.

Riding With Purpose

Beyond Saturday’s main rides, Ruta del Jefe includes presentations and workshops led by organizations working across the Arizona-Sonora Borderlands.

The event’s 2027 fundraising goal is $100,000, benefiting six organizations: Borderlands Restoration Network, Kino Border Initiative, San Xavier Cooperative Farm, La Tierra del Jaguar, Sierra Club Borderlands Program, and Sky Island Alliance.

The organizations’ work spans ecological restoration, wildlife conservation, Indigenous food sovereignty, migrant dignity, and environmental advocacy.

Participants are encouraged not only to raise funds but also to engage directly with the organizations and learn about their work.

A Different Kind of Cycling Gathering

Hosted at Borderlands Restoration Network’s Native Plant Nursery and Seed Lab, Ruta del Jefe centers community rather than competition.

The event combines camping, shared meals, supported riding, educational programming, cultural experiences, and live music in an immersive four-day format.

Registration is now open, with general admission priced at $595 and limited Access Fund tickets available for $345. Fully funded scholarships also support participation.

Ruta del Jefe 2027
April 1–4 | Patagonia, Arizona

See all the details and more at Ruta del Jefe.

The post Ruta del Jefe Returns to Arizona’s Sky Islands in April 2027 appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: ‘The best there ever will be’: India sets bar high for country’s first UCI World Championships in 2032
entry.content:
Cyclist
‘The best there ever will be’: India sets bar high for country’s first UCI World Championships in 2032

In 2032, the UCI World Championships will be held in India for the first time. Yet while the crown jewel of the international circuit will be more than a century old by the time Pune welcomes the Worlds six years from now, India’s sights are firmly set on it being an event to remember.

‘People will see the best World Championships there ever will be,’ says Cycling Federation of India’s secretary general Maninder Pal Singh. ‘We will also have the fourth Grand Tour here, Pune will have regained its spot as the bicycle city of this country, and India will become the cycling nation of the world as well.’

In other words, the bar is being set very high indeed. Pune is at the epicentre of cycling’s current boom in India. Historically known as the country’s ‘city of cycles’, Pune is looking to reclaim its crown in a future less dominated by industrialisation and vehicular-centric infrastructure. The city is situated in the western state of Maharashtra and is around 120km from Mumbai as the crow flies. It’s the focal point of the Pune Grand Tour, a stage race whose name hints at grand aspirations despite having been only held for the first time this year. And that after taking just six months to go from just an idea to riders heading off the start ramp for the 7km prologue on 19th January.

The Pune Grand Tour will expand to six stages for 2027 and has already been promoted from 2.2 to 2.1 status by the UCI, meaning its peloton makeup can be devised of no more than 50% WorldTour teams, putting it in the same category as the likes of Etoile de Bessèges, the Coppi e Bartali and O Gran Camiño. In its debut edition in January, the race kicked off with a prologue followed by four stages that took riders around Maharashtra thorugh Mulshi to Haveli, Nanded City and Baramati, diving through green valleys and traversing rivers, with overall victory going to Luke Mudgway of Li Ning Star.  

Clearly it’s a race very much on the rise, and Singh is firm in his belief that it will eventually develop into a fourth Grand Tour, even going as far as to predict it will eventually be considered the grandest of them all.

‘I can promise you, it is going to be bigger than the Tour de France,’ he says.

The implementation of the ‘Sundays on Cycle’ scheme by India’s Union Minister of Youth Affairs and Sports, Dr Mansukh Mandaviya, has highlighted the popularity of cycling in the country and its growing potential. In just under two years, these short weekly bike rides as part of a nationwide fitness movement have garned almost 3.7 million participants.

‘Dr Mandaviya has a special love of cycling,’ Singh says. ‘Before becoming a minister, he would cycle to Parliament, which is a rarity, and made sure he had a parking space for his bike – he wrote to the Speaker of the House to ensure it. When he became the Sports Minister, he wanted to begin a movement in cycling that encouraged more people to get on their bikes and just ride. You can’t imagine the amount of grace people have for Sundays on Cycle. It’s almost not normal. But people will ride every Sunday. It’s amazing.’

Sporting success in the nation in recent years has largely been propelled by the highly popular and lucrative Indian Premier League in cricket. In its footsteps comes the launch of the Indian Cycling League this November, in which eight teams of ten riders will represent eight different Indian states in rounds held across the country that each comprise a road race, a criterium and an individual time-trial. Of the ten riders in each team, two spots are reserved for international riders and another two for juniors, the rest being filled by elite Indian cyclists. The first round will take place in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, in western India.

‘It’s in a nascent stage,’ Singh says, ‘but I think what makes leagues interesting to people is the showbiz and the glamour factor that comes along with it. Of course, when you host amateur events, you can have your hands tied. Leagues allow for a little bit more legroom in terms of spreading your wings out and making it more spectator-friendly. They cannot only be a sporting success, but [need to be] a commercial success to sustain them for years to come.’

Women’s cycling is also flourishing in India thanks to the Khelo India ASMITA League. Created to promote grassroots women’s participation, it covers 37 sports disciplines including cycling, with road, track and mountain bike events held across age categories and providing cash prizes. There might not be any cyclists from the world’s most populous country currently represented at the highest level of road cycling in the WorldTour, but grassroots success is instrumental in promoting a sustainable growth towards this.

‘The bigger the base of the pyramid, the higher your pyramid will be,’ Singh says.

The Jakhar sisters are proof of the league’s success in capturing talent at the grassroots level. Harshita Jakhar won ten gold medals at the Khelo India ASMITA League in 2023, while the younger Anjali claimed five gold medals. The two would then be responsible for back-to-back bronze medals in the junior individual time-trial at the Asian Road Cycling Championships in 2024 and 2025. Harshita later became one of eight riders from the UCI World Cycling Talent Programme to lead a ceremonial neutralised ride before Stage 2 of the Tour de France Femmes in 2026. Her presence was noted by UCI president David Lappartient, who said he hoped for the 19-year-old to one day return to take part in the race proper.

It was Lappartient that first floated the idea of holding the World Championships in India ahead of it being officially announced in September. Back in June, when the UCI Management Committee meeting in Italy was considering upgrading the Pune Grand Tour to 2.1 status, Singh notes that Lappartient ‘in the middle of our case, told us we were doing good, but asked why we hadn’t spoken about a bid for the World Championships. We looked at one another and said, “well, why not?”

‘We thought, let’s take this opportunity. Let’s not waste it. We know our abilities and capabilities.’

The World Championships in Pune will be situated on roads that by then will have hosted the Pune Grand Tour through seven editions, ensuring the infrastructure’s ability to successfully host an event of this magnitude should be well established.

Preparations are already well underway, however the ultimate measure of the event’s success won’t be made when the final rainbow jersey has been awarded. This is a nation eyeing sporting superpower, and as such, an event of this magnitude will help bolster India’s bid for the 2036 Olympic Games, off the back of the 2030 Commonwealth Games being held in Ahmedabad.

‘Anything that brings India a step closer to being noticeable in sports is of course huge,’ Singh says, ‘We want to get our athletes not only on the start line, but we want to perform well as a nation and it’s important for us that other Asian countries do the same too.’

‘Our aim is to have the best World Championships that will ever be in 2032. I think it’s high time that we start believing India will become the cycling nation of the world,’ he closes. ‘That’s what we are working for. Nothing less.’

The post ‘The best there ever will be’: India sets bar high for country’s first UCI World Championships in 2032 appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Stand and deliver with Feedback Sports
entry.content:
Cyclist
Stand and deliver with Feedback Sports

Let’s face it, bike maintenance isn’t the most glamorous of topics, but when you’ve spent thousands of pounds on a high-end bike, investing in high-quality tools and equipment to keep it in fine fettle and running smoothly really is a no-brainer. 

Since 2004, Feedback Sports has been producing professional-grade bike stands, tools, storage products and other cycling hardware with exactly that notion in mind. Its products are trusted by team mechanics at the highest level of pro cycling, yet the company is equally focused on providing value, portability and durability for everyday riders too.

Feedback Sports was started in Colorado by CEO Doug Hudson, who had a background in engineering and fibre optics and had already set up a successful messenger bag and lifestyle brand. His true love was cycling, however, and this passion would soon give him a new calling: to create a range of precision cycling products aimed at dedicated riders, racers and skilled mechanics. Together with his wife, Lisa, Doug got to work on the company’s first product, the Feedback Sports Alpine Digital Scale, and from there things have only grown.

Made for cyclists

Today the company produces a wide array of products that have been researched, designed and developed specifically for cyclists. Its repair stands are robust yet lightweight, and are designed to be portable and easy to travel with. Its bike-specific tools are a mechanic’s dream, combining smart, precise design using premium materials with superior functionality and ergonomic ease of use. Its storage solutions range from free-standing options that keep your bike easy to access or wall-mounted solutions if space is at a premium.

The Feedback Sports product range continues to expand, informed by feedback from pro team mechanics and everyday riders alike, yet Doug and Lisa’s love of cycling remains at the company’s heart. It’s this commitment that has guided Feedback Sports for the past 22 years, and will continue to drive it forwards in the future. 

The right tool for the job

Essential items for every cyclist from the extensive Feedback Sports product line

Sprint Bike Repair Stand

£360 | Buy now

If you’re serious about bike maintenance, a decent repair stand is a must. The Sprint Bike Repair Stand attaches to your bike’s dropouts to keep its weight centred over the stand’s tripod base, yet weighs just 5.4kg and folds down to an impressively compact footprint for ease of transport. Its 360-degree rotating platform ensures quick and easy access to any part of the frame, and the rubber-coated end caps on the tripod’s legs keep the stand stable at all times. It comes with adapters for quick release and thru-axle standards, and is backed by a three-year warranty.

Modular T-Handle Kit

£220 | Buy now

This fetching toolkit houses a set of ten colour-coded wrenches – seven hex and three Torx – in a space-saving tool roll. The removable lateral bars allow you to mix and match the driver sizes, while the handles can be set to three different positions to make it easier to access hard-to-reach places. The CNC-machined tool bodies feel solid in the hand yet their compact length ensures the kit remains lightweight and portable. The tool roll is easily integrated into Feedback Sports’ larger Team Edition case, or can be wall-mounted on a peg board.

Range Click Torque Wrench

£120 | Buy now 

Durable, versatile and capable, the Range Click Torque Wrench may well be the last torque wrench you ever buy. It measures torque between 2-14Nm, adjustable in 0.17Nm increments, while the dual-sided window display scale caters for right- or left-handed use. The shop-quality fit and plastic-free head and handle ensure a solid and secure feel in the hand, and the unit comes with 13 high-quality hex and Torx bits in a neat PFAS-free fold-up travel case, with the whole package weighing in at just 278g.

Pneuma CC floor pump

£100 | Buy now

The Pneuma CC’s bold design certainly catches the eye but there’s plenty of substance to back up the style. It’s a premium floor pump – complete with long hose, wide steel base and easy-to-read gauge – but it also houses an internal air cannister that can deliver a burst of high-pressure air to seat a tubeless tyre. It can even help lift your bike when paired with Feedback Sports’ Pro Air Lift repair stand. Finally, a concealed storage space in the handle is handy for keeping additional tools within easy reach.

For more information about the full range of Feedback Sports products, go to ison-distribution.com

entry.title: Salsa Blackthorn 125 Review: I’m Buying this Bike – Travis Engel
entry.content:
The Salsa Blackthorn 125 is one of a growing number of moderate-travel bikes with immoderate geometry. But it’s also got a few tricks up its sleeve that are very Salsa, and evidently, very Travis.

I guess I spoiled it in the title, but this review is going to be pretty positive. That tends to happen when the bike I’m writing about was tailor-made for me and my mountains. The aggressive-125mm-rear-travel-140mm-front-travel-trail-bike category is very much my jam. And I would call it a category. The Esker Howdy, the Norco Optic, the Canyon Lux Trail (and the Spectral 125 that it replaced) are all in the same league. And all are in the top 10 bikes I’ve ridden this decade. I figured the Salsa Blackthorn 125 would be a shoe-in, but something left me a little doubtful.

Bike journalists often look over each other’s shoulders to learn about what’s trending and hear stories we might have missed. Pinkbike is usually my first stop as I sit down with my morning coffee. I’ve worked with a lot of the folks over there. They know their stuff, and I trust their opinions. And they were more than critical of the Blackthorn 125. They complained of harsh rear suspension, a low stack height, and short chainstays. But a western Canadian’s “harsh” may be a southern Californian’s “poppy,” even though they tested it in northern Arkansas. And stack heights can be fixed, and short chainstays can be fun. I had to see this thing for myself.

Salsa Blackthorn 125 Quick Hits

  • 125mm rear travel, 140 front
  • Also available in 145 / 160 version, convertible by swapping shock, yoke, and fork internals
  • 29” wheels only
  • Carbon front and rear triangle
  • Aluminum version available
  • Split-pivot linkage design
  • Coil-shock compatible
  • Two full-sized in-triangle bottle cages on all frame sizes
  • Integrated accessory strap
  • 33.8 lbs (XL, with Lyrik fork* and without pedals)
  • $3,499 starting price with aluminum frame and Eagle 70 Transmission
  • $4,799 as tested*
    • *Stock builds run RockShox Pike Select, not Lyrik Select as pictured

Salsa’s suspension flip chips default to their “high” position. That’s not often the case these days, and it was the first thing I changed. That got me a slack-for-the-category 64.4° head-tube angle and retains a steep-for-any-category 77.9° seat tube angle. The Blackthorn’s reach numbers are nearly a full rung higher than today’s standard sizing ladders, but I still stuck with an XL with a 518mm reach. And the XL’s 635mm stack is indeed on the low side. It’s 10mm lower than an XL Specialized Epic XC race bike, though the Epic’s head tubes are a bit tall for the category. And maybe there’s a reason the Blackthorn kept it low.

Blackthorn 125 (left) and Blackthorn 145 (right)

There’s also another flavor Blackthorn, with 145mm of rear travel and 160 front. It uses the same frame, but a shorter shock mount, longer shock, and of course a longer fork. Stretching the Blackthorn’s head tube another inch may have been a bit much for that setup. A bar / stem upgrade isn’t an enormous expense, but I wish Salsa had specced a higher cockpit on the Blackthorn 125. Its built-in capability deserves a more downhill-friendly posture. After all, this is a downsized all-mountain bike, not an upsized XC bike. But true to the Salsa credo, it’s still an adventure bike.

Salsa Blackthorn 125 Design Details

Two full-sized bottles! That’s at least 48 ounces of freedom! Sure, Salsa couldn’t quite get that ultra-low dirt-jumper silhouette, where the top tube leads straight into the seatstays. But who cares? Standover doesn’t matter until well past the front of the saddle nose, if it matters at all. There’s ample room for a 150mm dropper post on a size small, and probably more. I’m currently running a 220mm on my XL with room to spare. The storage space is worth the slightly bigger triangle. And then there’s that little triangle up front with an even littler strap mount.

Bottom three photos: Travis Engel

There’s nothing stopping you from strapping any object to any frame tube, whether or not that frame tube is designed for straps. But this mount does keep the strap in place while you’re handling that object. It’s a nice added convenience. It also just gets you thinking about what you could use it for. Same goes for the top-tube mount, which I still haven’t decided on. I did a couple rides with a snack bag, a couple rides with a double Wolf Tooth B-Rad strap system holding a handsaw, and I’m working out the kinks of some Fidlock accessories. I kinda wish Salsa had also added under-down-tube mounts. But again, nothing’s stopping you from strapping objects down there, either.

Cable routing is fully guided, including through the chainstays. I just swapped this bike’s brakes for a review, and I appreciated the ease of just pushing a hose in one end and seeing it come out the other. Also, kudos to Salsa for routing the derailleur housing through the top of the chainstay instead of the bottom, making for a smoother line and smoother shifting. And there are a few other little nice touches. Like, the forward shock eyelet runs directly on a thick hollow bolt, which is held in place with an expanding collet. There’s a little mud flap to keep debris from getting stuck behind the main pivot, and generous stay protection.

Then there’s Split Pivot. It’s a linkage-driven single-pivot where one of the pivots is concentric to the rear axle. With regards to pedaling and pumping, Split Pivot doesn’t do anything that any other design couldn’t. But it does eliminate the rear brake’s tendency to excessively compress the rear suspension. Split Pivot seems to have its supporters, with patens from both Dave Weagle and (in a legally distinct form) from Trek. But personally, I think Split Pivot is … fine. Brake interference just doesn’t annoy me on a ride. At least not in a way that I can pluck from the chaos and put into words. It stands out even less when the travel is this short and this supportive. Split Pivot didn’t make itself known for better or worse during my testing. But we’ve got more to talk about before I get to ride impressions.

Salsa Blackthorn 125 Spec and Value

Increasingly, we’re seeing brands set a floor of $5,000, $6,000 or higher for their carbon full-suspension mountain bikes. And aluminum options are becoming more and more rare. With that in mind, I think the Blackthorn 125 lineup is pretty reasonably priced, especially for bikes you can buy from your brick-and-mortar shop. My $4,800 test bike’s frame, suspension, drivetrain, and wheels are solid. No notes aside from its ugly color. Even the WTB wheels surprised me. Their OEM-only models have been kinda clunky in the past, but I’d happily ride these until they die. My only complaint is the mid-powered SRAM DB6 brakes. They’re great as a budget option, but not if you’re trying to push a bike to its limits.

The $3,500 alloy version has similarly good bones, and I’m glad the metal fans weren’t given bottom-tier suspension or an outdated drivetrain. But the clear standout is the $4,000 carbon version specced with previous-generation Deore, though it’s out of stock and the folks at Salsa couldn’t yet share their plans for that tier’s future. In fact, inventory is spotty on all models at the time of publishing, But this iteration of the Blackthorn is barely a year and a half old, so stocks will be replenished. And hey, maybe your local shop has one on the shelf right now.

Test-Bike Setup

I made a couple significant changes within the first week of having the Blackthorn 125, and they deserve their own subheading. I always swap out a test bike’s handlebars for my Doom Lucky Risers because their 14° backsweep makes a new bike feel more like home. But I also added my Ergotec High Bass stem to boost their already generous 50mm rise. I did a lot of experimenting with headset spacers, and I ended up with the 20mm stack shown here. It looks odd, and only taller riders will want to go this extreme. But unless you’re looking for a race-like posture, I recommend raising the bar.

Photo: Travis Engel

While the cockpit change happened before I’d even aired up the tires, my shock adjustments happened over a few rides. The first such adjustment was to start removing volume spacers. My RockShox-equipped model came packed with the maximum of four Bottomless Tokens. Fox-equipped models are working on a different scale, but they come stock with a 0.6 and 0.1 cubic-inch reducer, which is still a lot. Of course, a brand giving you more reducers is better than fewer reducers. You can just take them out. I recommend anyone buying this model give that a try.

Photos: Travis Engel

In both its 125 and 145mm configurations, the Blackthorn’s linkage is designed to be progressive. It works with coil shocks, and the flagship 145 model uses Fox’s large-air-volume Float X2 shock. After removing three—then all four—of my test bike’s spacers, I eventually got RockShox to send their Linear XL air can upgrade kit ($105), which increases volume. The standard volume spacers still work, and the air can itself accommodates a few more if necessary. I spent most of my time with that Linear XL air can with two traditional volume spacers to reel it back in a tad. And now it’s probably time to finally talk about how it rides.

Salsa Blackthorn 125 Ride Impressions: Climbing

With its initial shock-volume configuration, the Blackthorn’s rear end felt much like the Canyon Lux Trail I just reviewed. That is; like an XC bike. Peppy, but not plush. Even running just a hair under 30% sag, it felt more like a 100mm than 125. This wouldn’t be an unreasonable setup for heavier riders and / or riders who are especially allergic to bottom-outs. Even for me, it didn’t feel “wrong,” but it did feel like the shock could do a better job helping me out on the bumps without sacrificing much efficiency. The stock air can empty of volume spacers did just that. It allowed me to find a setup that bridged the gap between that XC pep and the cloudlike indifference I eventually teased out of the Esker Howdy.

That more supportive feeling suited the Blackthorn 125’s geometry well. The short chainstays help it respond quickly and precisely on punchy, technical climbs. And the steep seat-tube angle kept the front wheel reasonably well planted to the ground. I even slid my saddle back a little after we captured the beauty shots in this review. It feels quite natural on challenging climbs that demand high effort and high precision. When I had to twist around and over obstacles, it had a nearly trials-y responsiveness.

And the geometry is doing a lot of the work here. Again, there’s no hidden magic in how Split Pivot responds to pedaling force. The Esker Howdy’s Orion Link, the Revel Rascal’s CBF, and the Norco Optic’s high pivot all offered built-in flotation on rough, high-torque climbs. If you could keep your body weight steady, those bikes could remain stoically neutral in their travel. The Blackthorn isn’t the hoverbike they are. It favors support over suppleness, but that’s still a perfectly valid approach. Even after I switched to the Linear XL air can, I never got sucked into the late-stroke doldrums in the occasional frantic mash up a rocky shelf.

And on that note, I loved seeing a 30-tooth chainring. I hope that’ll become a trend in non-XC bikes. Beyond just giving a lower low end, it allowed me to stay in smaller cogs for longer for a straighter chainline. That ring also pairs well with the 165mm crank arms that all the kids run these days. Speaking of which, I can’t remember having a single harsh pedal strike on the Blackthorn 125. Even in the “low” setting, my feet stayed out of harm’s way. It was enough to make me wish Salsa had gone a little lower. It’d be a way to pad out the stack height and lean into the bike’s natural aptitudes on the descents, but let’s not get ahead of ourselves.

While very few bikes are bad at smooth climbs like fire roads and groomed singletrack, the Blackthorn 125 is decidedly good. That supportive suspension kept it from getting too floaty as I spun my legs, and I love a horizontally mounted shock for convenient access to the lockout. And the geometry helped here, too. This bike has the longest reach of any bike I’ve ever spent more than a minute on. It paired well with the steep seat-tube angle. I’ve long argued that the “cramped” seated cockpits of some modern trail and enduro bikes aren’t actually as inefficient as they’re made out to be. Sitting and spinning can be done while upright. But having my hands a half-inch farther forward did make high-torque efforts a little easier.

And let’s not forget the impact of all the on-bike storage. In the month I’ve been riding this bike, I haven’t carried water on my back once. That moved some mass farther forward where it couldn’t tug as hard on the rear shock. But it also moved it off my back, and by extension, off my saddle. Plus, it totally upends the packing paradigm. When your excess baggage doesn’t include water, it’s a lot lighter. That opens the door for more minimalist solutions like race belts or bib pockets. And once I make this bike my own, I’ll be sewing (or ordering) bags for it. And I won’t need both bottles during the cool, wet times of year, so there’s potential to repurpose one bottle mount for extra layers or food. It is an adventure bike, after all.

Salsa Blackthorn 125 Ride Impressions: Descending

And I think Salsa’s adventurous reputation has made it hard for the Blackthorn to get its messages across. Even though Salsa has always made “normal” bikes built for good ol’ Type-1 fun, its name is rarely listed alongside overtly adrenaline-focused brands like Norco or YT or Santa Cruz. That’s why the Blackthorn 125 surprised me so much. It rips.

Like most bikes with this combination of travel and geometry, the Blackthorn 125 keeps you on your toes while also giving you something sturdy to hold onto. But it elevates both of those traits beyond similar bikes. The sturdy thing you can hold onto is its geometry. Most notably, its uniquely long front-center. When I would charge full speed into a section that I absolutely knew would knock me around, there was an imaginary safety net exerting a gentle, calming force that kept me in line. It does nothing to damp the impacts that would be much more manageable with an extra 20 mm of travel. But it makes it so those impacts don’t matter so much.

This of course comes with a long reach measurement. If, like me, you use reach as your north star when picking a bike size, please resist the urge to size down. The seat angle is steep, so your cockpit should feel fine. But more importantly, you’ll have that extended runway when you’re at the blurry edge of this bike’s capability. If anything, look for a handlebar with more backsweep and / or a shorter stem. Maybe even browse our ultra-short high-rise stem listicle, which is also a great way to mitigate the bike’s low stack height

I can’t stress enough how much of a difference my absurdly high cockpit made. It further relieved the stress of those hard front-end hits because I could ride more through my feet and less through my palms. Speaking of my palms, I’ll restate that I’d have preferred stronger brakes with a lighter touch. But that’s an upgrade you can kick down the road. A higher cockpit is more important. It also made for a little more neutral front / rear weight bias, which complemented the Blackthorn 125’s natural flickability. It takes very little effort to briefly slide the back end out to line up for a turn or snake around a rock. That sentence appears in some form every time I review a bike like this, but it especially suits the Blackthorn 125.

One reason is that the frame is quite laterally stiff. That’s no surprise because the chassis was designed to accommodate an extra 20 mm of front and rear travel, along with the extra abuse that invites. There’s also that short chainstay. It provided a good sense of when and where the rear wheel would deflect if I broke traction, intentionally or otherwise. And it made it easier to get the front wheel off the ground for a quick manual or to initiate hopping over an obstacle. I vividly remember two scenarios where I came around a corner to find a freshly fallen wet branch laying diagonally in the trail. The Salsa Blackthorn 125’s slight twitchyness made those quick pop-overs more reflexive.

It also presented some extra challenge when I wanted to make it swiftly but safely to the bottom of the hill. And I mean that in a good way. The firm suspension and short chainstays demand a more hands-on approach in technical sections. This eased off a bit when I swapped to the Linear XL Air Can, which allowed me to access more of the travel more easily, And it of course didn’t compromise the have-fun-but-be-safe geometry. I’m sure a coil shock would take that even a step further. But I’m not sure which configuration I like better. The stock low-volume air setup certainly suited the bike’s playful character.

The Salsa Blackthorn 125’s rear end is not a rudder that you can sink into a wave and coast back to shore. It rewards precision. I guess an XC bike also rewards precision, and is also a challenge. But there’s an important distinction: The source of an XC bike’s challenge is concentrated in front of the bottom bracket, in its short front-center and low handlebars. The Blackthorn 125 (once you’ve fixed its stack height) puts it behind it, with firm suspension and short chainstays. I find that’s a lot safer. The shift from caution to panic is a lot less steep and sudden this way. But there’s still tension. Tension can be fun. It makes a descent more exhilarating and more rewarding. Nothing harsh about that.

Pros:

  • Capable geometry
  • Peppy suspension
    • The traits listed above are in perfect synergy
  • Two in-triangle bottle cages
  • Multiple storage options
  • Smart cable routing
  • Coil compatible
  • Stiffness and durability of a longer-travel frame
  • Can be converted to a longer-travel frame
  • Aluminum option available

Cons:

  • Rear suspension is less plush than some bikes in the already-not-very-plush 125mm category
  • Stack height should be higher
  • Short chainstays aren’t for everyone

See more at Salsa

The post Salsa Blackthorn 125 Review: I’m Buying this Bike appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Best Black Friday cycling deals 2026
entry.content:
Cyclist
Best Black Friday cycling deals 2026

Once November rolls around, the Black Friday deals start. This month is a great time to refresh your cycling inventory and replace items that have seen better days after another summer of riding. It’s also an opportunity to upgrade your setup so that you’re ready for a great year of cycling in 2027.

Finding the best Black Friday deals can be a chore, but here at Cyclist we’ve done the hard work for you, searching out the bargains that we’d choose ourselves in the pre-Christmas sales.

Read on for our pick of the 2026 Black Friday deals.

Hunt 44_46 Aerodynamicist wheelset

Was £899, now £539.40 at Hunt Wheels

The Aerodynamicist range is Hunt’s mid-priced wheelset and available in a range of depths, all with 25% off this Black Friday. The Hunt 44_46 Aerodynamicist is the middle depth option and carries over tech from the pricier Limitless wheelsets. With hooked beads, there’s wide tyre compatibility, while Hunt points out that the 22mm internal width allows owners to fit tyres from 25mm up. At under 1,350g for the steel spoked wheels, it helps keep the weight down too.

Cyclist staff writer Laurence Kilpatrick was impressed by the carbon spoked version of the wheels when he reviewed them earlier this year, rating them great value.

We have a whole range of Hunt deals on our dedicated Hunt Black Friday sale page. Hunt says that its most popular deals are already selling out though, so if you have your eye on a wheel upgrade, you might want to act fast.

Scott Shield Light Sensitive Sunglasses

Were £110, now £77 at Scott Sports

Scott’s Black Friday deals include these large lens Shield photochromic sunglasses, available either with a black or white frame. They feature Scott’s gold chrome mirrored lens, which darkens from Cat 1 to Cat 3, so they’ll handle the typical range of light conditions across different seasons. Single tint Shields are discounted as well.

There’s a whole range of other discounts in Scott’s Black Friday sale, from clothing to Syncros Capital wheels. With the brand’s broad range of sports, there are discounts on trail running and ski kit too.

Le Col Hors Categorie Summer Jersey

Was £165, now £99 at Le Col

Le Col’s Black Friday sale includes this top spec Hors Categorie summer jersey. Designed for endurance riders, the fit is a little more relaxed, while features such as a taped neck and embroidered logos add a touch of class and UPF 50+ sun protection should see you through the longest, sunniest summer rides.

Currently available in saffron only, the Hors Categorie summer jersey is part of a wide range of Le Col summer and winter kit on offer, with Le Col Cycling Club members offered early access to the pick of the deals.

Specialized S-Works Aethos 2

Was £11,499, now £8,999 at Sigma Sports

Sigma Sports has discounts on a wide range of road and gravel bikes including the Cervelo S5 and this top spec S-Works Aethos 2 in a range of sizes. Lower Aethos 2 specs are discounted too, although in a more limited range of sizes.

Laurence Kilpatrick rated the S-Works Aethos 2 when he reviewed the bike, not least its 6kg weight in size 56.

Sigma Sports has Black Friday deals on a wide range of clothing, components and accessories too, so chances are that if you’re looking for something specific, Sigma will be offering a Black Friday discount.

Ribble Ultra-Grit Force XPLR AXS

Was £4,449, now £3,999 at Ribble Cycles

Ribble’s Black Friday deals change each week, so if you’re looking for a new gravel race bike, now’s your chance. The Ultra-Grit is ridden by the Ribble Outliers pro race team and features aero tube profiles, a one-piece cockpit and in-frame storage. In this spec, it’s kitted out with SRAM’s 13-speed Force XPLR AXS groupset and Vision SC45 wheels. The frame is suspension fork-compatible and you can upgrade to a RockShox Rudy Ultimate XPLR fork, as well as Zipp 303 XPLR SW wheels in Ribble’s bike builder.

Ribble’s Black Friday deals extend to a wide range of its other road and gravel bikes too and Ribble guarantees that, should the price drop later in the Black Friday sale, it will refund the difference.

Garmin Rally XC200 SPD dual-sided power meter

Was £959.99, now £599.99 at Tredz

The Garmin Rally power meter pedals are discounted at Tredz, offering you dual-sided power measurement for Shimano SPD gravel cleats for not much more than the list price of the single sided power meter. They have swappable bodies, so you can change to an SPD-SL or Look Keo power meter for the price of the upgrade kit.

Tredz has over 1,000 products discounted for Black Friday, including Garmin smartwatches and cycling computers and Garmin Tacx smart trainers, so it’s a great place to browse for your replacements and upgrades.

Castelli Sorpasso Pro Bibtights

Were £220, now £176 at Castelli

Not technically a Black Friday sale, as it finishes on 16th November, but Castelli has discounts on its cold weather essentials, so you can gear up with its jackets, base layers, socks and other cold weather gear for both men and women riders.

The Sorpasso Pro bib tights are Castelli’s top spec winter legwear, with its Progetto X2 Air seat pad, zipperless ankles and lay-flat bibs, as well as the reflectives to keep you safer on your winter rides.

Tacx Neo 2T smart trainer

Was £860, now £689 at Balfe’s Bikes

Tacx’s high tech Neo 2T trainer is discounted at Balfe’s Bikes for Black Friday and is available with either a conventional 11-speed cassette or Zwift Cog and Click for the same price. With 2200 watts resistance, it’s plenty powerful enough, it folds away neatly and can mimic a 25% incline. It’s quiet too, that is unless you want to simulate riding cobbles in preparation for an early season Belgian sportive.

It’s one of a wide range of cycling equipment and bikes discounted in Balfe’s Bikes’ Black Friday sale, including turbo trainers and indoor bikes from Elite, Wahoo and Wattbike.

Muc-Off Pressure Washer Starter Kit

Was £120, now £84.99 at Decathlon

If washing down your bike after a winter ride feels a chore, Muc-Off’s pressure washer can speed things up. It comes with a range of lances, including one that allows you to attach a bottle of Muc-Off’s bike cleaner and spray your bike with grime-busting foam, making bike cleaning much more fun.

Decathlon has a tasty discount on the Muc-Off Pressure Washer Starter Kit, which comes with all the lances you could need and is housed in a Muc-Off branded dry bag, making it easy to carry around. There’s a range of other cycling equipment and bikes in Decathlon’s Black Friday sale too.

The post Best Black Friday cycling deals 2026 appeared first on Cyclist.
