entry.title: ‘It’s nice to enjoy the ride; it’s important’: Dorian Godon profile
entry.content:
Cyclist
‘It’s nice to enjoy the ride; it’s important’: Dorian Godon profile

Dorian Godon is not your typical pro cyclist. The fast-finishing Frenchman is constantly in motion, whether sprinting at 70kmh to WorldTour victory (five this year already), going paddleboarding and rock climbing, or shopping on his vintage bike. The world is there to be explored and life is to be enjoyed.

Splitting his time between Andorra and Girona, every day is an opportunity for adventure. Before racing this year’s Tour de France for Netcompany Ineos, Godon made the most of his ‘downtime’ around training by hiking up Pyrenean mountains with his girlfriend.

‘Sometimes we took a picnic and a book,’ he says. ‘I had the best raspberries I ever ate. The simple life.’

Godon has spent much of his sporting career studying physiotherapy and has a ‘completely different vision’ to most of his peers. Even a different look too, given the moustache he has maintained since the 2025 Tour Down Under.

‘It’s important to shave or clean it sometimes – I always have some food or whatever on it,’ he says, laughing.

It’s a case of ’stache and grab, as Godon has taken 13 pro wins since adding the fuzzy facial fairing. Get rid of it and maybe he would lose his Samson-esque source of strength.

‘Moustache is power,’ he once joked.

Indeed, vive la différence: at the time of going to press, no rider on Netcompany Ineos has more road victories in 2026 than the 30-year-old. All but two have come in the WorldTour top tier too, including a stage victory at Paris-Nice, a brace of sprint wins at the Volta a Catalunya, plus the prologue and a stage at the Tour de Romandie. He has enjoyed a seamless transition from Decathlon AG2R La Mondiale last winter.

‘I was surprised they had no stress, no pressure. Sometimes in French teams they push a lot. They [Netcompany Ineos] give you all the keys to do your best,’ he says.

In its Team Sky days, the team had a reputation for being robotic; Godon is anything but.

‘I thought it was like that,’ he admits. ‘Then I got there and saw it was super-familiar – no groups, everybody talking to each other and not about what they’d done before. There was no “I won this race and that race”. It was very humble. I was surprised – a good spirit to perform.’

Godon was attracted by the opportunity to try a foreign team after nine years with French teams Cofidis and Decathlon: ‘Maybe I didn’t have the maturity before,’ he reflects.

The race-opening Barcelona TTT at the 2026 Tour de France was already on his mind when he joined a squad that leaves no stone unturned in their preparation. In October, they spent time in the velodrome working on positioning.

‘I started to like doing TTTs again. I didn’t before so much,’ Godon says.

As it turned out, second place in the Catalan capital was the high point of the race for Godon. The route didn’t offer many opportunities for someone who says he is not a true sprinter and ‘prefers when it’s harder’.

On Stage 12, his Tour mission turned from seeking success to survival after a heavy crash in the final. Godon says it took more than ten minutes the next morning just to get out of bed, but the X-rays did not show anything and he soldiered on. It turned out post-Tour that he had fractured four ribs.

‘I couldn’t breathe. I went after Stage 17 to the radiography check and they did a similar thing. Sorry to say, but the medical directors are just there for the image of the race; the medical staff seem like they are on holiday,’ he says.

‘Maybe if I knew I had something serious, I would have DNF-ed, but I had already booked a restaurant in Paris so I had to get there. Every stage I said, “Just one more day to go.” It’s the Tour de France, I don’t like to DNF, it’s not in my spirit. But sometimes I should.’

Motivation can come in many different forms. His 94-year-old grandmother was waiting in Paris for him with his family, as was a special meal.

‘A friend of mine studied at a famous culinary school in France and he has a Michelin-starred restaurant, so it was a good opportunity to go there on Monday. I had that on my mind.’

Article continues below…

Always on the move

Being a top rider requires a lot more than hours in the saddle. Godon works out in the gym three times a week, and has been doing injury rehab for a crash that’s still giving him pain six weeks later.

Twice a week Godon uses his Exxentric box – a weight training platform that uses a flywheel for resistance instead of traditional weights – spending 20 to 30 minutes on it per session.

‘When you push and go down, because of the pulley you can’t stop. It’s good for explosivity.’

Godon says it’s especially good for working his back, strengthening the muscles that connect the shoulder blades to the spine. Then there’s core work, lifting weights and spending time on the exercise ball, something he demonstrates to Cyclist while juggling bananas.

‘Who doesn’t love bananas?’ he says. ‘We are all monkeys.’

After weights, Godon gets out on his bike, training on the quiet roads around Girona. Then afterwards it’s onto another bike – his grandfather’s Motobécane, which is over 50 years old – for a spot of food shopping around town.

‘The Motobécane is the most beautiful bike I have – sorry Pinarello. But Motobécane doesn’t exist anymore, so I can say that.’

On his vintage bike, Godon heads to the market for fresh produce, and he has his go-to local spots for meat, fish and yoghurt, eschewing big supermarkets. That extends to supporting his favourite bakery, La Puntual, where they often offer him a free cake when he stops by.

‘That’s why I’ll never be a climber,’ he says.

Godon is a gourmand, who loves pastries, Breton salted butter and cheese.

‘I won a race a few years ago in the Jura,’ he says. ‘They gave me 35 kilos of Comté. We shared it out behind the team bus for all the staff, but I still had 16 kilos left. I put it in the fridge and ate everything.’

Although the fromage made it onto the scale, Godon doesn’t weigh his meals at home.

‘I’m a little bit old school,’ he says. ‘I don’t even count calories so much when out for a ride. On hard ones I try to eat as much as I can. I’m not crazy about the numbers.’

After dinner he goes for a city stroll, and can be tempted by the ice cream shops – more than excusable given he burned an estimated 6,000 calories in training on the day he spoke to Cyclist.

Godon struggles to stay still for more than five minutes, which can lead to some rest day walks, barbecues or rock climbing sessions. He tried golf for the first time recently too.

‘The first shot was super-nice. I went, “Wow, this is easy.” I was close to the hole. And then after it was shit, always in the lake.’

Then there is pétanque, which he introduced to some of his teammates at a training camp after the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes.

‘It’s the French national sport. As a Frenchman, I always have the kit in my car.’

Mind, body and soul

When he was younger, it was the bike, not boules, that won his heart, although Godon says he took a scenic, pressure-light route to the pro ranks. Growing up in Lyon, he competed sparingly in the spring due to his focus on school.

‘My parents [an IT project manager and international purchasing worker] never pushed me. I have a completely different vision and that’s why I have a long career too, because cycling is part of adventure for me. When I was a teenager, on Wednesday afternoons friends and I would go out into the countryside, always exploring. And that is still on my mind. Recently [teammate] Thymen Arensman and I did a super-nice loop and found a new 5km gravel road. We punctured, but whatever.’

Godon claims that his approach to the sport is at odds with many of his contemporaries.

‘Pro cyclists look at their computers. I come across many who are in the airport most of the time and listening to their music; they cannot just listen to the birds or simple things. They need distractions. It’s a bit how the world is going, but I like nature. Even now, if I have five hours’ endurance training, I sometimes go on my gravel bike. I like to change it up – that’s why I’m never bored riding. I always say I’ll end my career when I know all my home roads. It’s nice to enjoy the ride; it’s important.’

As for training, he says, ‘I like the effort, suffering and everything, but I’m not a machine. I know some riders always do efforts on the same climb. I can’t do that. I’m not a robot.’

Despite some promising results as an under-23, Godon didn’t know whether Cofidis would give him a full-time contract for 2017. Having applied unsuccessfully for physiotherapy school in France, he saw one across the Spanish border in Girona and signed up.

‘I thought it could be nice to ride there; I didn’t know anything about the history,’ he says of Girona’s role as a cycling hub. ‘I always put study in front of riding and said, “There’s time.”’

Godon juggled education and perspiration. He cut down lesson time around races and did his required time practising physiotherapy between September and February. In all, the four-year course took him eight to complete, but not only did he get his degree, along the way he also met his partner Margaux, who is now a soigneur for women’s team Canyon-Sram.

Since focusing fully on cycling at the end of 2024, there has been no more waiting for Godon to fulfil his potential. Describing himself as a puncheur more than a sprinter, he has shot to prominence, with his long finishing kicks becoming a forté. Ultimately, he says, the eclectic life he chooses makes him happy.

‘It’s a super-nice opportunity to discover the world by bike and get paid,’ he says. ‘I like to be outside too, I live my passion, I do the job I want to do. I’m not a general classification rider so I don’t have to make a lot of sacrifices.

‘It’s more about travelling and training camps. We are away a lot – that is the biggest sacrifice for me. Sometimes I’d like to stay a bit more conservative or train at home, but for me this is the easy, simple life. I like it.’

Weighting for Godon

The training plan of Dorian Godon

Intensity, intensity, intensity: Godon’s most frequent sessions – apart from ‘going to the bakery’ – are lactic work and 30-second sprints. Short efforts build power for sprints.

Adapting to the calendar: ‘At the beginning of the year, everybody goes pushing in zone two on their training rides, then when I start again in August I’ll start in zone two then go for high intensity or work on specific capacity.’

Get the miles in: A big week of training for Godon is 24 hours in the saddle, with two or three gym sessions.

Work with the coach: ‘Adrián [López, coach] is super-human, not all about data. It’s a lot about sensations. Sometimes we call each other and we don’t even speak about cycling… I don’t want to have a data analyst, trainer or whatever. Even on the races, I’m not a climber so I don’t need to have numbers.’

And relax: Partner Margaux has also studied osteopathy so she sometimes gives Godon a massage, helping with the recovery after riding.

Fuelling the fire

A typical day’s food for Godon

Breakfast: Overnight porridge with Greek yoghurt, oats and milk. ‘Today I put in French jam and chestnut cream, which made it taste better,’ he says. Sometimes he has eggs and avocado on toast. Salty butter from partner Margaux’s home region of Brittany and his parents’ honey are a must.

Post-ride meal: Rice or pasta with salad. Godon has recently discovered Colombian delicacy arepas – a type of flatbread – thanks to teammates Egan Bernal and Brandon Rivera.

Dinner: On the day Cyclist visits, Godon has made a tomato and feta pie for later in the day. He eats a lot of vegetables at home, given the amount of pasta consumed for carb-loading in races.

The post ‘It’s nice to enjoy the ride; it’s important’: Dorian Godon profile appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: No Lugs No Masters: Romance is Dead by Crust Bikes
entry.content:
The team at Crust Bikes has been working on developing some new frames, including a stripped-down, more utilitarian build of the Romanceur dubbed the Romance is Dead ($1,225). These frames have no lugs, save for the fork crown, and are all TIG-welded. Because of this simpler frame construction, they’re a little cheaper, too. They feature a slightly sloping top tube and have a more robust downtube than the previous Romanceur frames, while maintaining the same tire clearance and geometry as the Romeo. TL;DR, no lugs, no masters; Romance is Dead.

Check it out at Crust Bikes.

entry.title: Weis MFG x Hunt Wheels x Larry Chen
entry.content:
The NYC-based frame builder, Weis MFG, and UK-based Hunt Wheels come together with renowned car culture and automotive photographer Larry Chen to build his dream titanium road bike to match his latest project car, a 1996 Honda Accord Sir with full 7-Eleven livery.

Debuting for the first time in person at the SEMA show in Las Vegas, Nevada. The bike matches Larry’s personal 1996 Honda Accord SiR with full 7-Eleven livery. The dedicated teams at Weis and HUNT brought the car’s unique livery and fine details to life in a fully custom paint scheme, Pantone-matched to the Accord.

The Bike – Weis Road Ti Ultralight

The Weis Road Ti Ultralight is the Brooklyn-based frame builder’s top performance machine. It pairs the elegance and lifetime reliability of titanium a carbon seat mast, uniting the most extraordinary bicycle materials into a one beautiful bicycle.

The Ultralight is built from custom-formed and butted, thin-wall 3AL/2.5V Titanium tubing, engineered for optimized ride quality, durability, and responsiveness that has defined our Titanium frames. The ovalized top tube and aero downtube, both formed in-house, create lateral stiffness to maximize power transfer and vertical compliance to keep the rider comfortable in the saddle on long rides.

Larry’s size 56 Road Ti Ultralight is the latest iteration of the model, and the custom paintjob matches to his ‘96 Accord.

The Wheels – HUNT 4AM Limitless

The HUNT 4AM Limitless, are the brand’s flagship road racing wheelset launched earlier this year. Engineered to maintain speed and composure whether on fast flats or high alpine mountain roads. By optimizing the balance between weight, aero drag, and stability, the HUNT in-house engineering team has set the standard for mid-depth road wheels.

Custom for the Larry Chen project, the team at HUNT collaborated with long-time partner, Ali Mclean at Fat Creations, to custom paint the wheels, adapting the HUNT logo to pair with the Honda branding of Larry’s car and to add a few of the car’s sponsors as an homage to the classic look and feel of the Accord. To tie it all together, HUNT opted for a fully polished silver Chase SL hub and silver spokes for this custom build.

The Car – 1996 Honda Accord SiR

Larry’s vision for this 1996 Honda Accord SiR was to combine Japanese, Thai, Indonesian, and US tuning culture together in one. What would it have looked like if 7-Eleven raced in the Japanese Touring Car Championship back in the mid-90s?

Check out more on the Ti Ultralight at Weis.

The post Weis MFG x Hunt Wheels x Larry Chen appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Grit Fest 2026: When The Homies F*ck With The Vision – Spencer Harding
entry.content:
In 2026, Austin Killips took the helm of the Bentonville-based nonprofit All Bikes Welcome. With only a few months to prepare, she scrambled the homies from all parts of her bike life to come together and make the “first annual 6th Grit Fest” happen. Austin invited Spencer to check out what happens when the homies fuck with the vision…

Now you might be thinking, “That is a lot of cussing for an inclusive nonprofit’s yearly bike gathering”, and you would be right, but it was a phrase Austin kept relaying to me over and over throughout my week in Arkansas, so let’s run with it.

Want to throw a silly scavenger hunt…call the homies who fuck with the vision.

Want to have a drag king roll in on an electric Tostitos scooter and dazzle attendees with jawlines and rose petals alike…call the homies who fuck with the vision.

Want to raise money to open a non-profit bike shop in Fayetteville…call the homies who fuck with the vision.

Need to screen print merch on thrifted clothing in your front yard…call the homies who fuck with the vision.

Want to host a group of deaf cyclists so they can attend MTB clinics…call the homies who fuck with the vision.

When your event coordinator slips a disk in their back the day before the event… that’s right…call the homies who fuck with the vision.

Welcome

I had never attended any previous Grit Fest events due to being a cis male identifying person, as the previous iterations were focused on catering toward femme, trans, and non-binary folks. I understand my place in the bike world and the very real desire for many events to focus on non-cis male attendees, as most bike events are heavily male-dominated. Hell, the first question I asked Austin when she invited me to come document the event was, “Can I come to Grit Fest?” She retorted that she planned to do something totally new with Grit Fest and, as the nonprofit moniker says, All Bikes Welcome. Trusting Austin wholeheartedly, I booked my ticket.

Our backdrop for the weekend would be Lake Leatherwood, about an hour’s drive from the Bentoville/Fayettevile area. Nestled in a low valley with trail systems on either side of the lake and a quick jaunt from Eureka Springs. The North side of the lake is dominated by the Lake Leatherwood Bike Park, a part of the OZ trail system, while the south side of the lake has less gravity-focused trails.

Friday evening featured a chill ride led by Ian Henrikson, who will be helming the future Fayetteville bike shop. We found that even a chill ride to the top of the Leatherwood trails was no easy feat. The berms and rocky sections of Shreddy Yeti gave a glimpse of the potential of the trail system. A quick downhill had us making our way to camp to make sure we didn’t miss the 6 pm keynote speech. The Keynote featured Austin from All Bikes Welcome, Bird from Wheel Mouse, and Biscuit from Cyclocross For Everyone. The talk outlined the vision for the weekend’s event and moving forward with All Bikes Welcome and how the new version of Grit Fest came together.

While I didn’t get a recording of the Keynote, I did ping Austin for an interview post-event of her talking points:

Why Did You (Austin And Team) Have To Build A Different Event?

Well, I can say that the shift was not at all my intention or expectation when I stepped into this role. I don’t think it is useful to get into the weeds, but the grant and funding landscape that sustained many inclusion initiatives across and well beyond our industry has disappeared or been reallocated to other projects.

For Grit [Fest] to exist in the coming years, we had to shift to being self-sustaining instead of an event underwritten by grant funding. So we took it upon ourselves to build an event that shares the same moral foundation and outcome goal of an inclusive and welcoming space for beginners and people underrepresented in the world of bikes, but embraced a different collection of design principles.

In our “keynote address,” we talked about the imperative of building grassroots events as foils to the seeming bubble economy of these large corporate events that so often feel like they’re built for everyone and no-one. Words like “grassroots” and “community” get lobbed around with reckless abandon by people who, for lack of a better phrase, like likes. My framework for a grassroots event is something realized by the participants. I think you can embed that in the structure and design of an event in many ways, but something very important to me and my collaborators in Chicago with Cyclocross For Everyone is distributing the means of event production.

If we want to continue building a healthy and self-sustaining event ecosystem outside of entities like USAC and Lifetime, attendees need to leave feeling both held by the space we built over the course of the event and empowered to go build something with their friends back home.

What Challenges Did You Face?

Oh gosh, well, there were a lot of challenges, Spencer. Have you organized an event like this before? I have not; it turns out they are really complicated objects, made more unwieldy when you have about six months to make it happen and less than half of the historical budget.

I think the biggest challenge came the week of the event. Our event coordinator, Bronwen, slipped a disc and was in the hospital with some serious complications, and the park manager of our venue was also out with the flu. Losing the two people that were involved in all of the planning meetings meant I was constantly managing the micro and macro of the event. But, watching our cohort of volunteers and friends come together to make everything run smoothly was this beautiful collective exercise. It was really beautiful to see this motley crew of longtime supporters and new friends of the org rally together to make an event happen.

Organizing an accessible event for our disabled friends at the event was also a totally new challenge for me. I feel like I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about non-sighted users and participants over the last few years, and this is obviously the inverse of that. We are fortunate to have Ciara Logan, a local deaf mountain biker and activist involved with All Bikes Welcome, to help us steer the programming and accessibility services on-site. I think we did a solid job this year, but I’m really excited to collaborate with our deaf attendees for 2027 on signing resources for all event attendees, optimizing the lighting so our interpreters aren’t bathed in moody shadows at key moments, and scavenger hunt challenges that explicitly encourage building connections across the language gap.

What Do You Hope To Create Looking Toward Next Year’s Event?

I want to fill Lake Leatherwood with weirdos on the margins: people who range from being bike curious to local rippers, but who largely share this experience of not quite feeling a sense of place at a lot of bike events. The scavenger hunt is a really fun way to build something with a low skill floor and a high skill ceiling for participants because it’s unwinnable and simply encourages you to go frolic and find a balance between pedaling and being creative.

I’m also excited to keep playing with all the silly performance art stuff. Eureka Springs is an island unto itself, but Northwest Arkansas is America’s neoliberal test kitchen, and I think it’s ripe for a ribbing. Next year will be our founders summit. Expect lanyards, a slide deck presented on a slide projector, a full update on our annual KPI’s, CSF’s, EBITDA’s, Q3 numbers, and more pencil skirts. Our success is your success.

Oh, I also want to host single-speed cyclocross worlds.

Is This The gayest Bike Event Of The Year?

I’m retired from competing in things, but I do think we made a very gay and transgender bike event. We had furries in our midst, a medley of genders, and a drag show. We’re not competing, but we could certainly be in the running.

I do think it’s important to build spaces for the folks who have been explicitly shunted out of this sport. If It’s not governing bodies banning us, it’s coordinated campaigns on the internet disseminating our likenesses to millions of cruel ghouls on the internet chasing any opportunity to draw blood. Even if we’re not barred from participation, trans people still have to ask whether lining up is worth the psychic wound of potentially being featured on the homepage of a right-wing tabloid. I hope we can become a space for some of the people who have lost a sense of place in the ecosystem of events that courted us and our money for years and then promptly caved to astroturfed social pressures orchestrated by organizations invested in making the world a worse place and perpetuated by people with corroded souls.

A Gritty Saturday

Saturday morning came quickly, and I found myself devouring baked goods from Shady Grove Farm Bakery and chasing them with some good ol’ Camp Coffee. The first half of the day was devoted to bike clinics, ranging from first touch all the way up to advanced skills. I joined the advanced class because I wanted to work on my jumps and drops since both are in short supply back home in Tucson. The ever-featured Leatherwood Bike Park had a plethora of man-made features for the group to sample and get rowdy on. I likewise wanted to be present to document a cadre of deaf cyclists who joined in the clinic. All Bikes Welcome hired two interpreters for the weekend to make sure the deaf cyclists could participate and keep up with all the activities. It was a logistical lift to get the interpreters way up on the MTB trails, but many thanks to our liaison from the Lake Leatherwood who…you guessed it…fucked with the vision.

The afternoon was filled with workshops, talks, and people scrambling around to complete their scavenger hunt manifests. I had a lovely conversation with Jen from the Mendery, a local Fayetteville gear mending business, which I plan to visit next time I’m in town. I picked up a fancy new bowl from Dark Horse Pottery, whose proprietor, Allison, was part of the team helping to screen print merch before the event. After plinking some cans with a slingshot, as the scavenger hunt called for, and a trip to walk along the lake, it was time for dinner. A plethora of platters and falafel filled the large table as everyone dug in.

Tostitos, an Electric Scooter Cooler, and a Schwinn Signed by Courtney Cox

Just before dinner, our entertainment for the evening arrived: Dr. J Maniac, who rolled in on an electric scooter/cooler, our drag king for the night. After everyone had eaten, the Dr. included, we formed a long line of chairs for Dr. Maniac’s performance. After a tambourine-and rose-petal-filled performance of Celine Dion’s classic “It’s All Coming Back to Me Now,” the raffle commenced.

As you can see, the prize table was stacked! Austin had to cut people off after they’d won two prizes. I was able to trade a shoulder bag and bar tape I’d won for the box of, personally, much-coveted magic cards! When a non-nerd won the Warhammer set, they graciously donated it to our chef for the weekend, who held up the massive box and proclaimed “FOR THE EMPIRE.” Everything wound up right where it needed to be.

Even the Grit Fest men’s, women’s, and non-binary winners were chosen by raffle in addition to the sprinter and climber awards. Anyone could win! Chicago did somehow sweep the top three spots of Grit Fest, maybe some raffle interference…

Once all the prizes, including a bike frame from Chumba, were dolled out, karaoke began. Thanks to Smith, most folks got to wear their sunglasses at night; their futures were looking way too bright…

Biscuit was nearly falling out of their chair laughing about the prospect of explaining to someone that our chef was singing “Not Over You” on a grass stage with a Tostitos electric scooter cooler and a Schwinn signed by Courtney Cox. This moment has never happened before and will never be recreated…

Holy Water Hardstyle

Sunday morning was likewise filled with a menagerie of baked goods washed down with Camp Coffee and a hearty platter of pancakes. Grit Fest offered up two ride options for the day: a 15 and 30 mile ride option. The 15 mile was mainly gravel and pavement with a small helping of single track, while the 30 had a larger helping of single track and a visit to nearby Eureka Springs. Having heard much about the lore of Eureka Springs over the past few days, I elected to try the longer ride, if only to see the famous Eureka Springs. With a toss of the sacrificial Specialized Vita, we were off…

An equally steep uphill and downhill brought our crew to our first aid station courtesy of the Gnargo folks. Camp Coffee had crafted coffee-freezy pops for the riders, which were an instant hit. As we got closer to Eureka Springs, I spied more pride flags and an equal amount of Jesus-y messaging. As we reached one of the famous springs near town, Thomas was nice enough to bless everyone as they took a drink from the healing spring. As we wound our way through the Passion Play trails, we eventually pedaled our way to the iconic Christ of the Ozarks. After paying our respects with wheelies and hardstyles, we hit the trails to get back to Leatherwood.

Our group mulled around until our last wayward companion, Kaitlyn, finished the whole 30 mile loop that most of us had cut short. We welcomed her back with a proper friend tunnel to close out the weekend. Caitlin was the only true finisher of Grit Fest 2026, praise be.

This year’s Grit Fest was a testament to what can be created in short order when you have a devoted group of homies you can call on to make shit happen, and happen it did. I left the weekend with a full heart and a bunch of new friends from all over. I am excited to see Austin keep up this amazing energy with some proper time to prepare and the subsequent bike shop in Fayetteville.

If you are looking at these photos and thinking, “I fuck with the vision,” keep your eyes peeled for Grit Fest 2027; I have zero doubts it’ll be a banger.

The post Grit Fest 2026: When The Homies F*ck With The Vision appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Spencer’s Favorite Bikes of Grit Fest 2026 – Spencer Harding
entry.content:
While attending this year’s new and rejuvenated Grit Fest, an inclusive bike festival hosted by All Bikes Welcome, Spencer picked a few of his favorite bikes from the crowd to document. He hit every wheel size, so no nerd will feel left out. Check what he found below…

Much like my coverage at Bike Camp earlier this year, I couldn’t fit the bike check in with all the coverage of the event, so you’re getting two whole articles. I have three bikes for your consideration, hailing from decades ago to a few months old, across the spectrum of wheel sizes, 26″-29″; all you 32″ haters can breathe a sigh of relief. Check out my favorite bikes from the Grit Fest weekend and the equally lovely humans who built and pedaled them.

Reese’s Gary Fisher Hoo Koo E Koo

Details, details, details, Reese’s bike begged closer inspection. With the rear brake posts chopped and re-welded for 650b, this Hoo Koo E Koo isn’t like the others.

Reese’s spare chain fashion bleeds into the build with a mismatched chain as well as a Deore XT lower cage hacked onto an XTR parallelogram. The hacking doesn’t stop there with her custom decauleur. The topo designs framebag perfectly mirrors the Velo Orange rack by becoming a mini pannier.

Purple anodized bits from Paul, Chris King, and Sim Works permeate the build, adding pops of color. I really love the faded ano on the Chris King hubs with an asymmetrical lacing pattern: 2x drive side, straight non-drive side.

With so many details and non part left unexamined, Reese’s Gary Fisher was an absolute favorite of the weekend at Grit Fest.

Dan’s Personal Pachyderm “Truck Bike”

Moving on to the most modern and largest-wheeled bike of my picks with Dan’s Pachyderm. Only after shooting this bike did I learn that Dan was the builder and sole proprietor of Pachyderm bikes. Dan’s personal rig is a slacked-out rigid 29er with a custom stainless steel front rack. Here is the geo if you wanna nerd out about it with Dan:

Initially, the Type-2-inspired fork caught my eye, but the overall stance and nice lines held my interest. The fork was made from “some old Columbus 26 in unicrown blades matched to straight gauge 1-1/8 in blades.” With a mismatched Boost front hub and standard 142mm rear hub (what he already had), mated to a 73mm BB, this bike is truly custom. The stand-off bosses on the seat tube allow for lots of dropper post insertion. The color is “frosted shamrock” sprayed by Blue City Cycles, an old shop mate of Dan’s from Chicago.

Featuring a cable-actuated connoisseur’s groupo with SRAM XX1 11-speed drivetrain, Paul Klamper stoppers. The Chicago crew really had a hankering for purple anodized bits, though Dan went less ostentatious than Reese with just some purple valve stems.

Dan’s rowdy rigid Pachyderms was perfectly suited for our longer single track laden ride on Sunday. Looked like a hoot and I can’t wait to make it out to Chicago and check out his shop and the rest of the Bubbly Dynamics freambuilding collective.

Mer’s Dean Titanium

In an effort to appease the vintage 26er restomod mafia, I hereby present Mer’s 26er Dean Titanium.

Sky-high bullmoose bars, check.

Headset pipe, check.

XTR hubs, check.

Matching Realm TT pad and water bottle, big check.

I got to watch Mer take this comfort shred sled out for a night ride around the techy trails of Lake Leatherwood. Undeterred by the small wheels, we were successful in our mission, if not covered in a few cobwebs. Mer has the distinction of being an outlier with the Paul 100% cranks, but they are at least square taper; we’re still in spec, y’all. The Avid Single Digit brake arms perfectly matching the raw Ti sheen was *chef kiss*.

Well done Mer, it was a pleasure to pedal around with you at Grit Fest.

Honorable Mentions

There were plenty of amazing bikes at Grit Fest, this is but a small vignette. I figured I should include a few honorable mentions: the Courtney Cox-signed Schwinn, the streamers and cat loving basket bike, and Dr. J Maniac’s Tostitos scooter.

The post Spencer’s Favorite Bikes of Grit Fest 2026 appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Trainer Apps Roundup Coming: Which Apps to Include?
entry.content:
It’s been a hot minute since I’ve done an indoor trainer app roundup, and in some ways the landscape has changed, and in others it’s kinda still same-same. The same major players are still all here, though consolidated a bit by who owns them. Still, the biggies remain – and include the likes of Zwift, TrainerRoad, MyWhoosh, Rouvy, FulGaz, Peloton, Tacx Training App, and TrainingPeaks Virtual.

But then beyond that there are basically three buckets of smaller apps, which I’d probably divide into the following categories (note I use ’smaller’ here in the context compared to the ones above):

Group A) Smaller-ish apps that have been around the block a long time but have a following: e.g., Kinomap, BigRingVR, Wahoo SYSTEM, Xert, etc…

Group B) Newer-ish smaller apps that have gained popularity or notoriety in the last little while: e.g., BikeTerra, Vieta, etc…

Group C) The gazillions of mostly AI-created trainer apps that vary wildly in concept/support/etc…

Now, with that said, one of the reasons I’ve fallen behind on keeping my trainer apps list up to date is that it’s mostly nightmare fuel to do properly. Sure, I could create a quick list of all the apps out there, pretend I rode them as most publications do, and then call it a review. Or, they just ask some AI platform to quickly make a list with some screenshots. But that’s not my style. I actually want to ride these apps, and there’s no AI-written garbage here. Many of them I’ve ridden already for years, either frequently or infrequently. So I’m familiar with some of them.

But there’s a whole lot of ones in Group C above that I’ve never heard of (and frankly, might disappear next week after someone stops paying a hosting fee). Some of these are totally wild (in a good way), and many of them are free. But tracking them all in my inbox is mostly impossible. Meaning, even if you’ve e-mailed me about them, I’d strongly recommend dropping it below in the comments too. :)

So, here’s the deal: To make this semi-manageable, I’ve already started on a number of apps to be included in an updated guide, and I’m gonna keep chugging over the next 7-10 days on riding a bunch of the newer apps. But, knowing there’s a lot of interesting apps out there, consider this open season for posting the app below in the comments section.

Anyone is welcome to post an app name and/or link. If you’ve created the app – cool, go forth! If you’ve ridden the app, I’m game too (and to hear your thoughts, good and/or bad). Deal?

(Note: Due to spam reduction bits, for non-DCR Supporters, I have to manually approve links, so it may take a few hours for your link-inclusive comment to show up).

entry.title: 20 Years of Circles in Nagoya, Japan – John Watson
entry.content:
In 2026, Circles celebrates twenty years of building cycling culture in Nagoya, Japan. Founded in 2006 by Shinya Tanaka, Circles and its in-house component brand, SimWorks, have slowly grown its online and physical presence in the Japanese cycling culture. Over the past decade plus, it has opened a new Circles Tailored store, launched RAL (Ride Alive), an Italian restaurant, Cerchi, and expanded its Pine Fields Market bakery. After visiting the shop during its ten-year anniversary in 2016, Cari and John wanted to return for its big 2-0. Read on for an expansive gallery showcasing all that the Circles lifestyle brands have to offer…

Ten years have flown by since Cari and I were in Nagoya, Japan, visiting our friends at Circles and SimWorks. A decade compresses and expands time with each visit, and the growth of the bike shop and the Circles brand family was on full display during my day spent documenting the flagship shop.

20 Years of Cycling Culture

This year, The Radavist turns 20, and like Circles, which is also celebrating its 20th, this company began during the track bike craze of the early aughts. The track bike brought about a new, alternative approach to cycling, centering around punk, DIY spaces, and culture building. Post-performance cycling has a way of being an incubator for grassroots growth in community spaces. The Radavist, at the time of its inception, was focused mostly in the New York City area, where I spent my weekends documenting Beautiful Bicycles, Shop Visits, framebuilders, and events.

Across the globe, in Japan, a similar growth was occurring thanks to the track bike. Two powerhouses of Japanese bike shops grew out of this moment in time: Blue Lug and Circles. The two shops have been largely inspiring for future bike shops not only in Japan but worldwide. Twenty years later, the movement that began with the track bike, or 競輪, has evolved into one of the most extraordinary movements in cycling.

Shinya Tanaka and his Sycip 26″ hardtail he had built in 2014

US Framebuilding in Japan

Shinya Tanaka first conceived of the Circles brand in the early aughts, driven by his love for alternative cycling culture, including the US framebuilder scene. Brands like Hunter, Retrotec, and Sycip caught Shinya’s eye at the North American Handmade Bicycle Show, and he thought, “Why can’t we have these brands in Japan, too?” So he worked to bring framebuilders and component brands like Chris King, Paul Component, and White Industries to the Japanese cycling market.

At the time, there wasn’t much US manufacturing presence in Japan, since the country had its own component manufacturers and framebuilders, but Shinya’s business idea was more than importing US brands to Japan; it was about bringing a lifestyle element to Japan’s post-performance cycling community.

Japan’s main cycling industry revolves around Keirin racing. Perhaps its most popular bikes are the mamachari – or city bikes you’ll see most people commuting on – but the lifestyle of the California brands was unlike anything going on in Japan at the time. While the early aughts saw a boom in urban cycling, thanks to the fixed gear and track bike craze, Shinya was thinking decades down the road, and he knew track bikes would bring more cyclists into Japan’s culture.

Rie and Shige, in 2016, at the SimWorks offices in Nagoya

Working with Japanese Manufacturers

As the Circles brand grew, Shinya found that his core Japanese manufacturer brands of choice – Nitto, MKS, Honjo – made exceptional products but needed a fresh look and marketing to reintroduce them to this new lifestyle of alternative cycling culture. Shinya worked with an in-house team of designers to launch SimWorks in 2009.

By taking core Nitto, MKS, and Honjo models and updating them for modern riders with fresh branding and design, SimWorks revitalized Japanese manufacturers and introduced them to a new generation of riders. As the brand grew, so did its spatial needs, eventually leading to the launch of the US division in 2018.

Tanaka-san is a multidimensional, passionate person who loves connecting cycling with art and food. In 2012, he launched Early Birds, a cafe on the ground floor of the main Circles building. Keita, a chef and cyclist, runs Early Birds alongside Nanako and Kenji and cooks up American-influenced dishes for the morning dining crowd who likes to linger.

Tanaka-san and Chris King at the People’s Bike Show and the whole team at Culture Club, 2016

Circles Nagoya: Ten Years Later

Our last trip to Nagoya was in 2016, and the three-floor space of Circles was bustling, housing SimWorks design offices, Early Birds Cafe, and two floors of Circles inventory. Over the past ten years, the Circles building has been through a flurry of activity. Like a Rubik’s Cube of spatial organization, the team at Circles remodeled the upper floors from a custom bike-building boutique into an outdoor lifestyle shop, where it debuted its RAL, or Ride Alive, gear.

Its Doppo bicycle line, a subsidiary of SimWorks, now has its custom paint shop on the third floor, along with an employee break room. On the second floor is the RAL outdoor gear store, and the ground floor houses the main Circles bike shop and Early Birds cafe. Tanaka-san’s vision for what his brand would become has evolved piecemeal over time, all stemming from the intentional move to place bikes at the intersection of art, food, and culture, giving it just enough water to grow slowly but meaningfully over time.

Radavist + Circles

My intention with covering this growth was originally planned to be a single story on The Radavist, but after covering the newest addition to Circles, the Circles Tailored shop, as well as the all-new Pine Fields Market, this story will have to continue next week.

To all the Circles fam, thank you for opening your doors to two travelers, showing us the vibrant community you’ve grown over 20 years, and giving us a cultural tour of your city.

For the readers of The Radavist, there is much, much more on the way, so stay tuned!

Arigato to the wonderful people of Japan!

The post 20 Years of Circles in Nagoya, Japan appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Circles Builds: Shinya’s 2014 Sycip 26″ Hardtail – John Watson
entry.content:
Over the next few weeks, we’ll be sharing builds from the Nagoya-based Circles bike shop. Starting it off with a very special Sycip 26″ hardtail Jeremy Sycip built for Tanaka-san back in 2010…

It all began with a fork. “I got the fork, new old stock, from a swap meet,” began Tanaka-san, as we chatted about his prized possession: a beautiful Sycip 26″ hardtail. “So then I asked Jeremy, ‘Can you build me a bike for this fork?’ and this is the result.” In the 1990s, moto manufacturer RS Taichi collaborated with Showa, a cycling brand, and produced a number of suspension forks in Japan.

On display here is the embodiment of the Circles approach to bike builds. Take a piece of Japan – in this case, the fork – and the Shimano components, and mix them into the zeitgeist of the global maker community.

Framebuilder Jeremy Sycip took the axle-to-crown dimensions of the RS Taichi Showa fork and began to design a bike geometry best suited to fit 26″ wheels and rim brakes. Recalling the order, Jeremy told me, “I found an old invoice, and it says retro MTB for Shinya.” The Santa Rosa, California-based builder used a blend of his favorite tubing, as well as his signature Sycip dropouts, Mountain Goat headtube rings, and his signature wishbone seat stays, complete with a 2¢ refund: two pennies are silver-soldered to the seat stay tops.

The standout detail on this vintage-inspired bike is the white rack, which is designed to support a small bag and bolts directly to the seat stay and cantilever bosses. Paul brakes provide the stopping power, along with Paul levers and Shimano XT components. A Nitto post, WTB saddle and grips manage the contact points. For tires, the Panaracer Smoke and Dart provide the traction, and gold Velocity Aeroheat rims laced to Chris King hubs add the bling factor. The cockpit includes 2014 SimWorks components.

A turquoise Chris King headset is the cherry on top of what has to be one of the sexiest vintage hardtails in memory…

Interested in a custom creation of your own? Check out Sycip Designs. Live in Japan and would like a curated build? Holler at Circles.

entry.title: Readers’ Rides: La Fourche Cycles 2026 Concours de Machines
entry.content:
For this week’s Readers’ Rides, we have builder Tom Even from La Fourche Cycles in South Burgundy, France, the 2026 entry to the 2026 Concours de Machines…

La Fourche Cycles

I am Tom Even. I am building bicycles in South Burgundy, France, under the brand called La Fourche Cycles.

I am working with steel and stainless steel, creating bespoke bikes with an approach focused on simple and essential aesthetics, trying to make the most pleasant and performant bike to ride for one person at a time. The 2026 Concours de Machines challenged builders to create a modular bicycle capable of seamlessly switching between a high-performance road bike and an adventure-ready gravel bike, while incorporating a luggage system designed for effortless one-handed use.

On-Off-Road

The bike presented here is deliberately simple and minimalist: only the wheelset needs to be changed to switch from one configuration to the other. With 700 × 32 mm tires for road riding and 27.5 × 2.2″ tires for off-road riding, this technical choice makes it possible to maintain a very similar overall wheel diameter between the two configurations, and thus to keep the same geometry for both types of riding.

The rear of the bike takes inspiration from road racing, with relatively short 415 mm chainstays that allow 48/32 chainrings to be fitted despite the 55 mm-wide tires used off-road. The front of the bike, on the other hand, is designed to tackle rough terrain, with modern gravel dimensions: a 71° head angle and 65 mm of trail.

The front end is relatively short in order to provide excellent handling and responsiveness, while allowing the rider to put weight over the front wheel and maximize grip when descending the hairpins of the Galibier. The 165 mm crank arms help optimize the rider’s position and eliminate toe overlap, even with the larger tires used in gravel mode.

Columbus tubing is used for the frame, with aerospace-grade chromoly tubing for the stem and truss fork assembly. The rear rack is made from stainless steel. The frame is assembled using fillet brazing and silver brazing. 8.4 kg in road configuration, with a conversion to gravel bikepacking mode in under 8 minutes.

Inclusive Consideration

One of the key considerations of the 2026 Concours de Machines was inclusivity. As part of a partnership with the French Federation of ParaSports, the brief encouraged participants to consider the interaction between the cyclist and their luggage. How could the bike’s bags be removed and installed using only one hand?

The four side panniers use a three-point Fidlock magnetic attachment system, allowing them to be attached and detached with one hand. The frame bag is equipped with magnets that attach directly to the steel frame structure. Two fabric straps with Velcro then secure the bag firmly in place. The top bag on the rear rack simply sits on the stainless tubes and is secured with an elastic cord that can easily be installed and tensioned with one hand.

To take one-handed usability even further and make opening and closing the bags easier, they are designed with a roll-top system closed by an elastic cord and hook. The rear rack itself can also be installed and removed with one hand: simply remove the two upper mounting bolts and loosen the lower bolts by a few turns. The lower rack mounting tab is slotted, allowing the rack to be inserted onto or removed from the two bolts already installed on the frame.

Look Twice

I recently developed a color palette for my bicycles, inspired by the color charts created by modernist architects and designers. The idea behind the seven colors of the palette was to create muted, understated tones that are somewhat difficult to describe. For example, the blue can appear almost green, the black is actually a deep blue, and the white is grey… I like the idea that someone seeing the bike passing by might have a hard time identifying its color or defining it too easily.

The idea behind the bike’s paintwork was to exhibit all the colors of the range at the same time. The color palette was developed with the technical support of System P, who also painted the bike.

The bike was awarded three times at this year’s Concours de Machines. It won 2nd place in the concours, the Best Craftsmanship Award, and the Peers’ Award.

Build Spec

  • The bags were made in collaboration with Gamory Cycles, based on advice from Studio Ricochet
  • Drivetrain: mixed Shimano GRX and SRAM Red, 12-speed, with a 10–33 road cassette and 10–36 off-road cassette, and Extralite derailleur pulleys
  • Crankset: Praxis Doon GR
  • Power-meter pedals: Favero Assioma Pro MX2
  • Wheelsets: custom-built by Duke
  • Rotors and brakes: Galfer rotors and Hope RX4+ SL calipers
  • Handlebar: Ascent Aeroo
  • Headset: Extralite
  • Seatpost: Mcfk
  • Saddle: Prologo

 

We’d like to thank all of you who submitted Readers Rides builds to be shared here at The Radavist. The response has been incredible, and we have so many to share over the next few months. Feel free to submit your bike, listing details, components, and other information. You can also include a portrait of yourself with your bike and your Instagram account! Please shoot landscape-orientation photos, not portrait. Thanks!

The post Readers’ Rides: La Fourche Cycles 2026 Concours de Machines appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Counting Milestones at GRUSK – Andy Karr
entry.content:
Set amongst ancient rock formations and a million acres of National Forest, the Gravel Ride Up Spruce Knob has become a fixture of the mid-Atlantic gravel circuit over its decade of existence. Andy Karr brought his gravel bike, a camera, and two dozen of his closest friends up to the Seneca Rocks and Spruce Knob area of West Virginia to celebrate a series of big life milestones at this year’s GRUSK.

That the Gravel Ride Up Spruce Knob fell on my fortieth birthday was serendipitous. GRUSK has been a popular event for me and my Great Eskape teammates since 2017, and we’ve routinely made a weekend of it. We usually set up camp for our teammates and other friends for Friday and Saturday nights at the nearby Seneca Shadows campground. A weekend of camping, riding bikes, and hanging out around a campfire sounded like a great way to ring in decade number four.

Forty being widely held as a milestone birthday, a fair number of friends, family, and coworkers have asked me if I “feel old” turning forty this year.

Old? Wanna know what’s old?

The quartzite and limestone that now make up the distinctive geological features on Spruce Knob and the nearby Seneca Rocks in West Virginia are formed from sediments deposited on a seabed 450-600 million years ago. The spines of Seneca Rocks are sedimentary layers upended and turned 90 degrees on their side by the collision of a chain of volcanos (now the Blue Ridge) with the North American Plate over 200 million years ago. Nothing sets the anxieties of middle age into a proper deep-time context like holding a birthday party in a setting shaped by tectonic and erosional forces over hundreds of millions of years.

For the last ten of those years, the Gravel Ride Up Spruce Knob has been bringing adventurous cyclists together for a weekend of gravel riding, camping, and companionship in the middle of the Spruce Knob-Seneca Rocks National Recreation Area and its many crags and hollows (pronounced “hollers,” around here). In addition to hosting West Virginia’s tallest point, the Spruce Knob area is crisscrossed by streams and rivers, plentiful blankets of rhododendron and laurel flowers, nearly a million acres of Monongahela National Forest, and by hundreds of miles of gravel roads and doubletrack that make for endless possibilities for gravel riding routes.

Travis, GRUSK’s founder and (along with his wife Rachel) principal organizer, has been riding bikes in the Spruce Knob area since well before the term “gravel bike” came into wide use. Though getting to fishing spots was the primary reason for his earliest cycling adventures in the area, a precursor to GRUSK came about at the invite-only New Year’s Eve Ride Up Spruce Knob in 2010.

Evolution of GRUSK

The idea for GRUSK itself was born on a birthday ride. Travis rode to the top of Spruce from Seneca Rocks with a good friend for their birthday, during which they schemed up a gravel event on Spruce. Shortly thereafter, another promoter failed to launch a proposed 3-day stage race on Spruce Knob. Travis offered to help pitch in, and before he knew it, he was planning the first GRUSK.

This year was the 10th running of GRUSK. Over the last decade, it has evolved and changed as the “gravel scene” has changed around it. GRUSK was run for years as the Gravel Race Up Spruce Knob, but the infusion of hypercompetitive, more road-race-like attitudes and the worry of racing on open roads with traffic and blind corners weighed heavily on Travis and Rachel. Eventually GRUSK evolved towards a granfondo-style event with competitive segments, to eventually the non-competitive fondo style it is now.

The shift in approach not only meant a safer event, but also a shift in resources away from prize purses and towards improving the experience of all riders. Travis tells me he fully expected the event to die once the competitive element was removed, but the year following the transition to non-competitive actually had a boost in ridership over prior years. I think I speak for the vast majority of GRUSK riders in saying that it’s one of the most exceptionally well-run aid station and rider logistical experiences of any event I have done.

The route itself has shifted over the last decade. As the bikepacking format gained popularity, longer and longer routes have been added to the trio of single-day distances. The route design has also been altered to improve rider safety by avoiding some of the sketchier road descents and high-traffic stretches. In earlier years the route summited Spruce Knob near the end of the day – however, both careless drivers in rented jeeps and thunderstorms are much more common on Spruce in the afternoon, so the summit was moved to earlier in the day.

I’ve ridden GRUSK five or six of the ten times it’s been run. I know substantial changes have been made over the years, but they’ve not impacted the character of the route enough for me to really notice. It’s a beautiful route. It’s challenging without being grueling. I’ve done the 50-mile version, the now-defunct 75-mile version, and the 89-mile version – always scaled to my level of fitness at the time – so no year stands out as particularly hard or easy. As a bike ride, GRUSK has been consistent and dependable, bordering on ritualistic. It’s a fixture in the yearly ride/race schedule for the team and me. But GRUSK is, and has always been, more than just a bike ride. It’s been a good excuse to get the increasingly geographically dispersed and busy-lifed gang together, see old friends, and throw down for a long weekend in the woods.

The Core of GRUSK

It’s all possible thanks to Travis, Rachel, and their small army of volunteers and local fire departments. Between the local bike shops that have supported the event with prizes, neutral aid, and even dry places for the bikepackers to rest, the local residents who wave and cheer us on throughout the ride, and the support of local leadership in working with GRUSK and its riders to fuel a growing outdoor tourism economy, GRUSK has been a catalyst of community building for a decade. I asked what running this event for the last decade has meant to Travis.

“Over the years, GRUSK has meant doing something bigger than yourself, building a community and showing the beauty of West Virginia to the cycling world beyond mountain biking. GRUSK has meant hard work, lots of long nights, and the usual blood, sweat, and tears event management brings. GRUSK has also meant thousands of smiles, dirty finish line hugs, campfire stories, and so many kind words from riders about the event. The results have been incredibly rewarding. I’ve strengthened friendships, forged new ones, and worked through differences in opinions to bring a quality event to every participant.”

Reflections at This Year’s GRUSK

GRUSK’s tenth year running was the perfect catalyst to draw together some communities of my own. Also celebrating tenth anniversaries this year are the bicycle club I co-founded with some of my best friends and DC’s Coffee Outside Ride series, which I’ve been attending since its inception in 2016. GRUSK 2026 falling on my 40th birthday this year meant that the group campout at Seneca Shadows was more than just a team affair – it brought together friends I’ve made through Coffee Outside, Great Eskape teammates, a ragtag group of other bike friends, Sarah, our dog Indie, and friends who’d be unlikely to sign up to ride up the side of a mountain.

Most, but not all, of us who camped together rode GRUSK. It was the impetus for all of this, after all. But the weekend was a lot more than a bike ride. We gathered around campfires, jumped into chilly swimming holes, cracked out our favorite camp stove recipes, marveled at fireflies, and joked and laughed deep into the night.

Gathering at GRUSK, and the decision to celebrate some big milestones there this year, laid bare some important reflections about the last decade. All the team rides, campfires, mugs of coffee, and front porch hangs offered more than a good time and memories. They connected people. I cherish the friendships I have made over the last ten years of this very bike-centric lifestyle. I am also immensely proud of the friendships these folks have made with each other at everything from events like GRUSK to semi-weekly coffee rides.

This community has really tied the last decade together, and I’m feeling upbeat about how it will grow, strengthen, and evolve.

As for GRUSK, rumors are that this may have been the last running of the event. I asked Travis after the event what the future holds for him, Rachel, and GRUSK. He said that the future was ambiguous.

“This may not be the last year of GRUSK, but it is the last year Rachel and I, along with our core group of friends, manage the day-to-day operations. It takes an immense amount of time and work to put on GRUSK every year, and the timing feels right to pass the torch over to someone with more time and energy to take the reins. We hope we can find the right person/company who will commit to keeping the spirit of GRUSK alive… We’re planning a small group tour to Italy in spring for the Strade Bianche and another small group tour to go watch and ride the routes for the first week of the Tour de France. There could be another gravel event in the future or maybe a gravel camp; we have lots of ideas, but who knows? We’re just going where our wheels lead us.”

The post Counting Milestones at GRUSK appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Scottish Mixtape Pt. 1
entry.content:
A self-supported mission to link 3 classic cycling routes and 3 peaks in Scotland.

In partnership with Arc’teryx, Moots Cycles, Tailfin, and Skratch Labs.

Words by KYLE RICHARDSON · Photos by THOMAS WOODSON, KYLE RICHARDSON


Exploring a place by bicycle works its way deep into your soul. Once you’ve traveled this way, it becomes your beacon and north star for how you want to explore the world. Taking in the landscape pedal stroke by pedal stroke, you start to learn the fabric of a place. Feeling the weather and terrain isn’t just one aspect of the outing; it becomes your identity and sole purpose for moving. The reward for moving your body all day through a place is knowledge and wisdom, things you can apply towards future trips and life in general.

Scotland is world-renowned for its rugged and beautiful landscape. Its people are hardened by the weather, but their desire for exploration and adventure in the hills is very much alive. There is a deep mystery about this place that is intriguing to me. The craggy tracks and alpine roads cutting through magnificent mountains planted a seed of curiosity. What would it be like to travel through this place simply? On bike and on foot, carving our way through this ancient country. Thus the Scottish Mixtape was born — a fully self-supported mission to link up 3 classic cycling routes and 3 peaks. From Scotland’s capital, Edinburgh, we traveled over the famous highlands, traversed the Cairngorms, and then down the Pictish trail, creating a big, diverse loop.

For the purposes of organization and to showcase this route, I will break the mixtape into 3 separate tracks, each corresponding to the 3 cycling routes we explored.

Filmmaker and photographer Thomas Woodson was alongside me for this Scottish adventure. This wouldn’t be a bike blog without digging into the bikes, and I will touch on setups a bit throughout. Thomas was riding his Moots MXC, and I was on the new Moots Womble, both bikes equipped with front forks and dropper posts for maximum shredding and efficiency. As always, feel free to drop a comment or email if you have more specific questions about setups, and I will include full bike check photos at the bottom. Sit back, grab a tea or a pint, and listen to the play-by-play from the Scottish Mixtape.

   

Track 1: Into the Highlands

Our bodies are stiﬀ and creaky. It’s really 3 am Colorado time as we depart our flight into Scotland's capital, Edinburgh. I think the biggest stressor for a trip like this surrounds traveling with a bike. This topic alone deserves its own blog and write-up. Needless to say, our bikes made it, and soon enough we were building our extremely capable mountain rigs in the crowded airport arrival terminal. Thomas must have snuck some coﬀee in somewhere, because by the time I was getting organized, he was ready to roll. Dang, time to get with it! I was distracted by the bright lights and stream of people passing by.

Handlebars, wheels — straighten it up - wait, tinker again, fix. Okay, is this right? Thomas! “I need help!” Good thing we make a great team. I have been adventuring with Thomas for a decade now. We have traveled to many countries together and mesh super well. Finding a partner that complements you and brings out your best self is a wonderful thing. Outside of being strong in the mountains and competent on technical terrain, Thomas is a logistical wizard and has an everlasting attitude to get things done no matter the circumstances. These are instrumental attributes on a trip with so much uncertainty and the unknown. We have a tight timeline. We need to be back in Edinburgh in 8 days to then catch our flight back to Colorado the following day. Okay, enough of this, time to hit the road!

Moots all built up at Edinburgh International Airport

In classic Scottish style, as we roll away from the hustle and bustle of the airport, the skies open up. The wind picks up in a fury, and we put on our rain gear. This would be the first of a long trip- a long process of navigating and handling the weather. Under my hood and amidst the rain, I crack a smile and let out a giddy laugh. This is why we are here. To experience the full spectrum of conditions and emotions of traveling through a new place. Our first day of riding would almost exclusively be on canal and bike paths; what a treat! One of my goals for this trip was to get oﬀ the main roads and into the magic of a place. And by magic, I mean all the sneaky little roads that take you to the heart of place rather than around it. As we worked our way towards Callander, we got to experience the canal boats and farm lifestyle that make up this part of the country. Riding through tunnels and lush forest, we sneak glances at quaint villages and ancient cobblestone paths. At one point during another wave of rain, we pass by a school. It was clearly lunch break, and all the teens were out walking towards their favorite hangouts. In the pouring rain, we noticed that no one was wearing raincoats. Huh. Are we doing this wrong? Rain and being wet is a way of life in Scotland; not much fuss about the weather. Go do your thing and get on with it!

By this point in the day, we had linked into the famous GBDURO (Great Britain Divide), a cycling route that covers the entire length of Great Britain. We would use this route to help carry us North. We traversed our first fields of Scottish livestock and enjoyed varied riding on all types of surfaces. Our bodies still on Colorado time, we visualized and dreamed about our first proper. Bopping and weaving around more farms, we could see our first stopping point of the night in Callander. A beautiful little village right on the edge of the highlands. We had booked a night at the Crown Inn, knowing that a real night's sleep in a bed would help set us up for a successful trip. Thomas and I love to play games, but when it comes to bikepacking, we generally adhere to a few basic rules and let the rest go with the flow. We see what the land and weather give us. This trip wasn’t about how hard and brutal can we make things; it's about the full-body and mind immersion into a landscape. We have our notepads out and want to learn and grow from this place. Students of the world traveling by bike.

One of the beautiful things about Scotland is how popular and welcoming the people are to bikes. People tour here on bikes, and it's not a new thing. You won’t get any strange or random looks. You will get chirps of encouragement and curiosity. The hotel staﬀ and BnB hosts will welcome your dirty bikes and bike shoes and have a safe place to store that stuﬀ, either in your room or a dedicated indoor bike shelter. I think this way of life helps cut the tension and edge that one can have while traveling in a new place, especially when your body is depleted after a hard day of pedaling. After sorting ourselves in our lodging, we slipped on our running shoes and headed out to the streets of Callander for some fish and chips. Thomas and I exchanged stories from the day as the native language and tongue echoed through the dining hall. Mates bantered about golf and what pint to drink next; we quietly observed our surroundings as our new reality for the next week set in. With our bellies full, we enjoyed some sunset light while strolling down the River Teith. It was a hectic and full-on first day in Scotland. Time to dry out our clothes and get some rest.

Moots arriving in Callander Day 1


Alarms chirping at 5:45 am, the hot water kettle starts bubbling, and we tear open our instant craft coﬀee from Idle Hands Roasting. The little morning treat that brought us energy and psyche every day. Thanks to Peter Jones for the full trip supply! Skies were grey and overcast, with mild temps. After hunting down some classic Scottish pastries and goodies down the street, it was time to set oﬀ. Our day would start oﬀ following the GBDURO to the small town of Killin, before branching oﬀ towards the mega-classic West Highland Way — (Scotland’s premier long-distance walking route, stretching 96 miles (154 km) from Milngavie (just north of Glasgow) to Fort William in the Scottish Highlands).

A misty collection of clouds started to form as we made our way north along bike paths, contouring lochs and villages. It felt special and unique to be on such fantastic bike infrastructure, tucked away in the woods. After a couple of hours of spinning, we reached a tiny pass, and the skies started to open up. As we stopped, we came to our first interaction with the famous Scottish midges. Tiny microscopic flies, coordinating in unison and buzzing towards their next victim. I could feel their wrath as we stopped to put on our rain jackets and pants. Maybe it's better if it's raining? At least then the midges subside. More to come on that later. As we buzzed down to the town of Killin, we had our first proper feeling of being completely saturated with water. My giddy smile and laugh from the day before started to flatten.

Thomas Woodson on film above Loch Lyon


In the town of Killin, we rushed towards the first cafe in sight. Was this a storm that would pass, or something that was hugging the mountains and would be around all day? Only time would tell. No use looking a weather app or forecast, it was unreliable and inaccurate. In classic Scottish style, we ordered a few breakfast teas and some toasties (basically a grilled cheese with a sweet chutney). Thomas and I slipped out of our wet cycling shoes and air-dried our feet discreetly under our table. As we were eating, a pair of cyclists showed up in similar fashion. Good reminder that this is totally normal and what we were doing wasn’t anything extraordinary. They were from Poland on a similar grand adventure (albeit on gravel bikes) out taking in the wonderful countryside.

For us, it is always encouraging and enjoyable to chat with folks along the way and feed oﬀ the energy of a place. Our new Polish cyclist friends seemed to have a determined edge, and we ended up sharing a similar route for a few miles. As we hit some steep grades, I think they started to grow jealous of our mountain bikes and gearing. As we soft-pedaled up our first real mountain pass, I was grateful for our setups and the terrain we were about to encounter. While never truly quitting, the rain turned more into a soft mist, which is far more favorable than a straight downpour. Our views were limited at the top of this pass, but I could tell we were on the cusp of getting into the good stuﬀ. Remote, wild, and properly in the highlands.

As we traveled around the south side of Loch Lyon, we rode premier double track. The kind of tracks I dreamed about, my inspiration for putting this whole trip together. Riding the right bikes, with the right person, everything was falling into place. Steep grassy hillsides, sheep, Highland Coos, countless river crossings- this section really had it all. Quintessential Scottish riding. Beams of sun would occasionally pop out and highlight a magnificent hillside. My giddy smile and laugh returned. Thomas was on the same page, and we hooted and hollered around each bend. Finally able to let loose and ride our mountain rigs with some flair. Being out in the wild, tucked in the mountains, felt like being home in Colorado. This is where Thomas and I thrive. At the end of this double track segment, we started a long downhill towards Kinglass Cottage and the West Highland Way. It was pretty obvious once we were on the WHW, as we immediately started passing thru-hikers. As we traversed the hillside, we set our sights on our next pitstop: Bridge of Orchy.

In classic logistical Thomas style, he had found a semi-secret stop for dinner, just a ways past Bridge of Orchy. He had made a call during lunch to set up a dinner reservation. We planned to stop in Orchy, grab a pint, then roll down the road for dinner plans. After dinner, we would continue on the WHW and find camp somewhere. I think trips like this require you to act fast and think on your toes. No one decision is ever that hyper critical, but make a decision and then go with it. I think having a good partner helps this process. Sometimes it's easy to get lured into a resupply or waste time. Finding the balance between riding the flow and making calculated decisions is the game. On this Day 2, we played our cards right and were rewarded with a fantastic day of quality and diverse riding. At dinner, we enjoyed one of our best meals. Sometimes best on a trip like this equals quantity, but at this fine establishment, we were treated with massive portions and delicious food. We even had a first tasting of some local whiskey. Felt rude not to sample!

Throughout the day, we had heard rumbles of evening and overnight torrential rain. Let me skip to the chase. Yup, that happened. We ended up riding maybe 3 miles to one of the few clusters of dense trees in the area. All of the Highlands is barren due to centuries of deforestation. Which means finding a good bivy site that is protected is tough. I think most locals would have laughed at our sleep setup, but I think I still stand behind it. Between us, we shared a flat tarp and ground sheet. Individually, we each had sleeping pads, bags, and bug nets. It appeared most people camped out in the open with proper enclosed tents. Hmmm. So we were oﬀ into the dense woods and mossy floor for a tucked-away bivy. I like feeling cozy even if it has its downsides. An exposed tent out in the open just feels wrong, especially on a night forecasting torrential rain and high winds.

Sleep was on and oﬀ. Out of the whole trip, this was one of the harder moments. The rain was persistent and loud against the Dyneema tarp. I also don’t want to gloss over the fact that just a couple of hours earlier, I was being eaten alive by midges. It was the Scottish gods (and maybe Thomas) seeking sweet revenge on my trip and idea. Making sure you never walk away unscathed, gathering a few lessons to learn along the way. In some aspects, the heavy rain eased my tension and pain. As we would come to find out later on Day 3, which proved to be one of the grandest and hardest day yet. Despite the rough night, we still had the energy and stoke to keep pushing. Waking up in the mist, Thomas and I remarked back and forth how intense that was.

morning wakeup ritual with Idle Hands Instant coﬀee


Moots on the West Highland Way


Awake and caﬀeinated by morning cold brew in a running soft flask, a few bites of something go into the body (not to mention the bites I was nursing on my body). We pack our wet bikes and gear inside fully waterproof Tailfin bike bags, proving their weight in gold. For me, I think it was seeing the sun that morning. It provided me the internal stoke and confidence to complete this trip. The light and scenery were otherworldly and magical. Entering the Glencoe valley was what dreams are made of. Giant peaks and ridges in all directions. We stopped for breakfast at one of the few ski resorts in Scotland, the famous Glencoe Hill. Full Scottish breakfast and coﬀee for me, please. The midge welts on my face and arms burned and itched. This felt like a warm trap to stay here all day, and I’m glad we were both motivated and stoked to keep the pace up.

Back on the bikes, feeling small. Coming around the corner, seeing Buachaille Etive Mòr (Stob Dearg) is a top 3 moment of the trip for me. This perfect pyramid, erupting out of the earth, was visually too perfect. How could something like this even exist? It was full steam ahead to our next objective, our first scramble of the trip, Curved Ridge. I first heard about this route when I saw an iconic photo of Kilian Jornet Burgada scrambling up Curved Ridge during his 2017 win at Glen Coe Skyline. Ever since then, it’s been on my tick list. One of the anchors of this project was to link 3 technically interesting running and scrambling routes in Scotland. Curved Ridge proved to be indeed a mega classic. As Thomas and I approached this massive pyramid of a peak, we could see a series of twisting ridges jutting up towards the summit. Clouds were swirling and rays of sun stabbed through the sky. It was now or never. As we approached the trailhead, the scale of this mountain started to introduce itself. We stashed our bikes against a climbing school hut, switched into our running kit, and set oﬀ. I’m always full of stoke and excitement when switching to running oﬀ the bike. The legs feel wonderful with a new motion, fresh to carry us up the peak.

Starting up the iconic Curved Ridge


Curved Ridge was everything you could ask for. Exposed, steep, airy, with wonderfully solid rock. As we ascended higher and higher into the clouds, the moves got more interesting. Culminating in a steep crux with plentiful holds and jams, Thomas and I motored our way up this aesthetic feature as a light mist set in. The view of the valley floor as we climbed up seemed mystically low and far away. As we reached the summit, the perspective we were rewarded with was hard to describe. That sweet satisfaction after biking for 2.5 days and lots of hills; the trip and vision were all coming together. After a few summit photos, the clouds swallowed us up, and the wind said hello. Okay, time to get oﬀ this thing! Running back down was a techy treat, practicing some quick footwork to navigate many a slippery rock and chunky talus. When it was all said and done, despite feeling like a full day's adventure, we were back at the bikes in 2 hours. Plenty more time for adventure and progression in the day.

Back into bike shoes, we grabbed our rigs and crossed the road. Next up was the most infamous section of the West Highland Way: Devils Staircase. From the summit of Stob Dearg, we could see the Staircase. Coming from Colorado, Thomas and I are accustomed to hike-a-bike (HAB). Some of our favorite local rides include HAB. I’m on record saying multiple times that all good adventure rides need to have some HAB. Despite the hype, Devils Staircase made us feel at home. No big deal really, maybe 30 minutes of pushing at the most? Come on! That is light work for us, even after a 2-hour run. The thing that challenged us really in this section was the weather. It was raining pretty hard for the rest of our day. Towards the bottom of the Staircase, Thomas had a rear tire slash while riding over one of the many water bars that line this climb. If my memory is correct, this was the only bike mechanical issue we encountered all trip. One of the benefits of doing a trip like this with a partner is that bike mechanicals and problems are so much easier to solve as a team, especially when the weather is bad. Couple plugs, add some air, back on the trail!

We made fun work of that climb, hiking with our heavy rigs past many thru-hikers. Showing them who is boss. At the top of the pass, we then proceeded to encounter our gnarliest true MTB terrain of the whole trip. Rowdy riding and chunky terrain. It was a brake-squealing, arm-pumping descent down to Kinlochleven. We were reminded once again that our bike choice was 10/10. I was thinking to myself that if I had been on my fully rigid ESC, I would have walked that entire descent. The trip would have been nearly impossible and stupid on that bike. Hardtail mountain bikes for the win!

In Kinlochleven, Thomas and I hit the local grocery store for some orange soda and a bag of chips. Something on the lighter side to fuel us over the next pass to Fort William. In some ways, I think we both thought our day was close to ending; little did we know we had some brutal climbing and weather to contest with. Oh, and some really rough and muddy tracks. The day was starting to add up. Waking up in our wet bivy spot just some hours earlier felt like a lifetime ago. Eventually we made our way up a steep mixed-surface climb and started a long gradual service road to a small pass that gave way towards Fort William. The riding here was tough and tedious.
